speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext: In view of the report which has appeared in the press referring to government intervention in the matter, has the Prime Minister any information to give the house with respect to the news report today as to a shortage in the funds of the Civil Service Co-operative Credit Society Limited and what steps have been taken by the government to deal with it?

maintopic: CIVIL SERVICE CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY REQUEST FOR INFORMATION AS TO REPORTED SHORTAGE IN FUND
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance
can perhaps answer that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CIVIL SERVICE CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY REQUEST FOR INFORMATION AS TO REPORTED SHORTAGE IN FUND
speechtext:
I saw the news report this morning. The Civil Service Co-operative Credit Society Limited is a credit society incorporated under the province of Ontario Credit Unions Act. It has been in existence for some forty years, I believe, and has some 9,000 members all of whom are federal civil servants. A short time ago it was discovered that there appeared to be shortages in the funds of the society amounting to some $120,000 or $130,000. The government, of course, is not in any way concerned, directly or indirectly, with the management of the society which is operated under the act to which I have referred; but it has an interest in the affairs of the society because all of the employees
are government employees. When the matter was reported to me it was indicated that the society proposed to take steps to investigate the management, auditing system and so on in order to ascertain what had caused the shortage; and as will have been seen from the press report this morning, a strong committee of senior civil servants has been set up to that end.
It is not clear yet what has caused the shortage but I think there is a pretty fair assumption that it has been inadequate bookkeeping methods over a considerable number of years; and it may well have been due to an improper setting up of profits which had not in fact been earned.
In any event, when the situation was reported to the government it was decided that, on the condition that the society take steps to see that its affairs were properly handled, the government would recommend to parliament the making of a loan to the society of up to $100,000 at an interest rate of 4 per cent, repayable in instalments out of profits. That is the position at the moment.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had finished my remarks last night and only asked for the adjournment of the debate in order to protest against those members who shout "time" to you and who now have delegated themselves to be the keeper not only of your conscience but of your clock as well.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when he introduced the motion under discussion, the Secretary of State for
External Affairs
External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) made a thorough and comprehensive report on the international situation and dealt particularly with our relations with the United States, South America and the commonwealth, outlining the government's policy in its relationships to those countries. He gave also detailed information as to the government's attitude on Korea, the situation in the Far East, and in southeast Asia, and he wound up his report with the problems facing NATO and the Canadian attitude with reference to them.
I think the house and the country will agree with most of what the minister said and, by and large, we all can. rejoice that Canada's policies are dictated by good judgment and by a cautious approach to every new development in world affairs; and also with courage and vision, assuming a firm attitude when required.
We are all in agreement, I think, that our over-all role should be the maintenance of peace in the world so that our country may continue to develop harmoniously and with the gigantic strides it has taken in the last ten years. But we are also determined to do our share to see that peace is secured by taking all the steps judged necessary to deter any nation from attempting to dominate the world. The minister has earned our approval and appreciation for the share he has played in drafting Canadian policies in international affairs, and for the role he has played on the international scene, as well as for the lustre that is reflected on Canada through his well deserved popularity and authority in the councils of the United Nations.
I have pleasure also at this stage in saying a word of appreciation of the part played by the member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) in his capacity as chairman of the external affairs committee. His career should stand out as an example to many young men who aspire to enter politics, as well as many new members in this house. Over the years the hon. gentleman has literally made himself into a worthy parliamentarian, and he deserves the highest consideration from his constituents, from his province and from this house.
Before entering upon the main body of my remarks, I should like to sound a note of caution as I did last year about the danger of accepting too readily the leadership of our neighbours to the south in international affairs. For too long a period of her existence has Canada been bound by British policies when this country was under the tutelage of that great power. For far too long have Canada's policies been based on British policies or influenced by British

External Affairs
interests since we have become of age. For far too long, in my opinion of course, this state of affairs has been more of a burden than an advantage to our country. Knowing how serious the consequences of being tied to the policies of a great power may be, no matter how friendly that power might be, we should be more than cautious today not to put ourselves in the same relationship to another great power. Surely we have not disentangled ourselves from the cobwebs of British international interests to tie our fate to policies that are made in Washington and about which we are not even consulted.
Of course Canadians realize that, in a world split into two spheres of influence, their own interest lies with those with whom they have the most in common and with the country whose economy has most impact upon theirs. Most Canadians have sympathy and understanding for their powerful neighbour but they would not relish the idea of playing the role of a satellite any more than the people in the satellite countries of the Soviet must like the role their country is called upon to play. It is hoped that the new administration in Washington will not overlook the advisability of dealing with our country with all due care and attention. In this way they may be certain that they will gain more friendship from a partner frequently consulted than from a reluctant or hesitant follower.
Canadian policies, Mr. Speaker, should be made in Ottawa, having in view Canadian interests and the commitments made by us in the interests of the preservation of world peace. I, for one, was favourably impressed by the cautious way in which the minister touched on the situation in Korea and the Far East during his speech. It is to be noted, Mr. Speaker, that Canada is committed to its share of the policing activities of the United Nations in Korea, and that is as far as this parliament has authorized the government to go. The statement by the minister that the guiding principle of Canadian policy in. Korea is to do everything possible to restrict the present hostilities to the Korean peninsula was a renewed assurance of Canada's position that will meet with wholehearted approval in the country.
I should like also to call attention to another statement the minister made which has the approval of most Canadians. He said, as recorded at page 1853 of Hansard for February 11, 1953:
We do not believe, accordingly, that the western powers should press for military or economic measures, at the United Nations or elsewhere, which would certainly not be supported and indeed might be actively opposed by important non-communist Asian states, and which without such support wculd be less effective in ending the Korean war than in extending it.
[Mr. Picard.1
And later on the same page he said:
It is, of course, very natural indeed to desire to hit the aggressor in new places and with new weapons, but it is also wise to realize that in consequence he may also hit us somewhere else and with new weapons.
The path, Mr. Speaker, between the desire for peace at all costs and the desire to see our cause triumph at all costs is narrow and full of dangers. In the first instance, we would agree to some bargaining, and in the second instance we might contribute to the doom of tomorrow, because no victor can emerge from the next conflict and enjoy his victory.
However, my object in rising today was not so much to expand on what the minister had said as to make a few remarks on the conditions that prevail in other parts of the world, and which may have a bearing on the maintenance of peace. In a situation such as that which has prevailed in the world since the end of world war II, one cannot overlook any of the events or problems which may, in one way or another, worsen the chances of preventing a new world conflict. Nor should we forget that the events in the world may depend on the outcome of other moves that may be made from time to time on the chessboard of the world.
One of the spots where problems may be less acute at this moment, but no less important than those prevailing elsewhere in the world, is the Middle East. When the politburo chose Korea as the testing ground of American resiliency, shall I say, there is no doubt that many spots were considered, and that the Middle East, particularly Iran, was one of the possibilities. The fact that they chose Korea should be a cause of satisfaction for us but not of reassurance. Our satisfaction must come from the fact that the Middle East is much more vitally important to us, and that the situation there may still be saved. But we should not be reassured until the proper and necessary steps have been taken to improve and consolidate our position in that area. These steps will demand more understanding and more determination to co-operate and help than has been shown in recent years by Britain, and more positive, friendly action than has already been taken by the United States.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I find myself in the awkward and delicate position, in order to substantiate the views I have reached, of giving the house an account of a trip I undertook in the Middle East last fall. In the course of this trip I had the privilege of meeting most of the outstanding statesmen in that region of the world. If the house will bear with me for a moment,

I	shall give a few highlights of my journey, and mention some of the people I interviewed, before I come to the conclusions I have reached.
I might say, first, that all but one of the interviews I had I arranged myself upon reaching a capital by calling directly the secretary of the official I intended to see or in some instances the protocol section of the foreign affairs department. On such occasions I stated that my trip was purely personal, but that as a member of this house I would eventually report to it or to the external affairs committee. In each case I was received with the utmost courtesy, and I would say cordiality. Everywhere I found that Canada enjoys the highest consideration in that part of the world, and this may be explained best by using the words of one of these statesmen, who said:
Canada entered two world wars without being threatened in its territory; it did its share nobly without any other motive than that of sharing in collective security measures; it helped others in time of stress; it reaped no material gains in return. It hurt nobody because it had no expansionists aims, whether territorial or commercial. It is not surprising therefore that it still enjoys the consideration it well earned by its conduct.
Be that as it may, I must say it gave me great pride in our country to experience the warm hospitality and the greeting I received everywhere.
Before proceeding to the Middle East I spent about three weeks in Greece and Turkey where I had long interviews in Athens with Mr. Venizelos, the then minister of foreign affairs, and in Ankara with the foreign minister, Mr. Koprulu. In Teheran I met Mr. Navab, the then foreign minister, and Mr. Mabil the permanent under-secretary, as well as members of parliament and generals of the army. Unfortunately my appointment with Premier Mossadegh was fixed for a date on which it was not possible for me to return to Teheran. In Baghdad I met the acting minister of foreign affairs, the permanent deputy head of that department and the British ambassador. In Beirut I was received by President Chamoun, and also had an interview with Mr. Hamid Frangye who was twice a delegate of Lebanon to the United Nations. In Damascus I had a long talk with Colonel Shishakly, who led the coup of 1948 and is the recognized leader of the country. In Amman I was received by the prime minister, Tewfik Pasha Abuluda, and in Israel I had luncheon with the foreign minister Mr. Sharett. In Cairo I spent over an hour and a quarter with the prime minister, General Mohammed Naguib.
I apologize for this long reference to the personal contacts I established in the Middle 68108-122J
External Affairs
East but considered it better to do it that way so as not to refer later to any of the personal and sometimes candid and open statements made by some of these statesmen and leaders.
The first and consoling conclusion is that none of these leaders favour the advent of communism in their part of the world and that none would like to see Soviet expansion be the result of the actions of their governments. Most of them favour a form of mideastern entente connected with or related to a Mediterranean defence pact, but none would favour his country entering it unless it be on terms of absolute equality of status, and in the case of Egypt only when any form of external influence in the shape of occupational troops or otherwise has ceased.
None of them thought that the U.S.S.R. would attempt any violation of any territory in the Middle East unless a general war developed in the world. Some of them recognized the danger of communist uprisings or communist-inspired parties gaining power, but significantly enough none admitted this danger to exist in his own country.
As to the Israeli-Arab feud, both sides profess that they observed the armistice terms and that the other side did not. All expressed the conviction that the conflict will not flare up anew, but while Israel professes that it would be ready to sign a peace treaty along the lines of the armistice terms with minor modifications of frontiers, the Arab states do not appear to be ready to go that far at this moment.
There is a strong trend towards nationalism and a distinct suspicion of, and antagonism to, outside pressure or influence throughout the Middle East.
The result is that if there is distrust of the Soviets, there is not on the other side any particular sympathy for Britain, France or the United States. Britain is decidedly most unpopular in Iran, Israel and Egypt. France has lost popularity in Lebanon and Syria on account of the happenings in Tunisia and Morocco. As to the United States, they dominate the whole area commercially but they have gained yet no true sympathy.
Statesmen expect much from United States leadership but seem to think that the United States lacks understanding of their problems and of the mentality of their peoples. There is a great opportunity for United States diplomacy in the Middle East but much will depend on the personnel sent there by the new administration and by their approach to local situations.

I have met statesmen who have said that Russia will never invade any of these coun-;ries. Why should they? One by one nany of them might fall prey to inside communist influences. The only one where the danger is actually present is Iran, and I ;hink it is high time that the situation was ;aken in hand and something was done about it.

had been told that the German ambassador vas supposed to see the general right after ne. In spite of that, however, I was brought a and told that there was no hurry.
The general showed considerable interest i Canada, and a better knowledge of this ountry than one would expect. I might add that I was favourably im-iressed by the general's unassuming, sincere md unselfish attitude. Despite all that may tave been said as to his dispensing with the onstitution for three years, I have become onvinced that he is devoid of personal mo-ives, and that his intentions were really to five his country a more democratic form of ;overnment, after the purification of the >resent parties.

The situation in Egypt, I need not remind hon. members, is such that out of a population of 20 million about half a million live decently, while the rest are on the verge of poverty. Without any wish to insult the relatives of any former ministers in that country, it was generally understood that to enter the cabinet ensured the fortune not only of the minister but of his friends and relatives.
The present prime minister said, himself, that one of the main endeavours in his work was to make sure that the same condition would not prevail in respect of the new group taking office. He pointed out that a reform of the civil service would take considerable time, and that we could not expect any radical change in a short time.
I was in the country to a point as far removed as the border of Sudan, and talked to many civil servants including judges and crown attorneys in rural districts. They all expect that within five years' time we will see a great change brought about by Naguib and his government. None seemed to think that the propaganda spread by the Wafdists and other enemies of Naguib proved that Naguib is a puppet in the hands of a few who run the country.
It is true that the movement came first from a group of young men in the army, many of whom were disgusted with conditions in the Egyptian army during the Palestinian war, and many others who just had army training and felt that they could do some good by helping to bring about a reform in the government of the day.
Those men at one time chose Naguib as the one most likely to gain popular favour, and the one whose advent at the moment would best bind the group together and strengthen it.
I must assure the house that the general opinion throughout the country, certainly among those people in different classes to whom I have spoken, is that the man himself is no fool, and that he is not the puppet of anyone. I came to the same conclusion after talking with him. The reform in Egypt came first in the agrarian laws, which I have read entirely, but the explanation of which would take too long. These reforms are earmarked to bring about better conditions throughout the rural classes, while not depriving the agricultural industry of the machinery already existing.
Personal holdings, for instance, are limited to 200 acres. Formerly holdings were as high as 50,000, 100,000 or 150,000 acres. Of course some will say that the breaking up of these vast domains which were operated in some instances with modern machinery

would work against the progress of agriculture in the country. The law provides however that in such territories as were administered as a unit the machinery shall be co-operative, as obtains in the great co-operative organizations in our own country, so that the people may share it.
Loans are to be given to these people. Owners are supposed to be repaid within a period of twenty years out of the rents the farmers will pay for their farms.
At the time I was there the two great events were the agrarian reforms and the agreement on the Sudan question. I saw yesterday that an agreement has been made with the British government concerning Sudan, an agreement more or less along the same line as the one that had been reached with the Sudanese themselves, except that in the first agreement they had the opportunity of choosing between complete independence and union with Egypt.
In the first one they were supposed to take that decision within three years in a plebiscite. In the new agreement there is added the possibility, according to British news agencies, of their joining the crown or staying with Great Britain through having some form of government under the British crown. But that is a minor point, in the end.
The important point was to let the people of the country determine the future of their own country: they were the ones to decide.
I might say this, that the reaching of that agreement, the unification of the people of the Nile, the throwing out, if I may use that word, of the outsiders, was the scheme claimed to be one of the great achievements of the general at the time.
During conversations the general said, "I am not anti-British. I recognize what they have done. I also recognize that over the last seventy years they have said from year to year that they were going out. They have not started to go out yet. I do not necessarily demand that they go tomorrow, but I would like to be sure that within a period of five years the country will be entirely free of outside troops. The reaching of that end can be studied and considered peacefully by the two countries."
Far from being an extremist or decidedly anti-British, I found the general to be very broadminded on all such questions. I found him to be well informed on all international affairs. I am one who thinks-and there are many others who are of the same opinion- that the present conditions in Egypt are for the good, and would bring about a betterment in the administration of the country, as well as of conditions throughout the country generally.

However, as was pointed out to me by some more democratically inspired statesmen during that trip, it is to be deplored that because of the lack of timely reforms the pattern developed in some of these countries in terms of a strong army leadership and undemocratic government. But, at this stage, to many this seems to be one of the necessary evils to counteract communist influence.
The leaders I met all professed and proclaimed that their aim was to promote an efficient restoration of democratic institutions, and they believed this to be possible only after a general purification of the former habits of autocratic governments which were democratic only in appearance, and in the hands of a few privileged leaders who ran the country only for their own selfish interests and those of their friends and families.
I had intended to talk about certain matters concerning the internal administration of the department. I think however that at this stage I shall leave the discussion of those matters until the (committee on external affairs sits. There is one thing though that I should like to say, before I take my seat, by way of a suggestion to the minister. Wherever I have entered a Canadian embassy abroad I have never seen a picture of the Governor General or the Prime Minister of this country. In some places they have a picture of the former King and Queen, probably the new Queen now, but after all we are a country that has institutions of its own and I do not think it would be considered political propaganda to display a picture of the Prime Minister and one of the Governor General, because with our institutions-let us hope i1 will take a long time to come

prime ministers may change and parties may change Therefore there is no political aspect involved in the suggestion. When foreigners enter our embassies I think it would be good for them to know that we have a representative of the Queen and that we have a Prime Minister. So far as suggestions are concerned that is as far as I will go at the moment with respect to the internal affairs of the department.

friend and one which was richly deserved. It was a tribute to Canada too, but since the minister has had no small part in the formulation of Canadian policy perhaps it can be construed indeed as a double tribute.
In his absence the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) made what I considered to be an admirable chairman. My appreciation stems partly from the fact that never at any time was I refused information which I wanted, and in large part because of his insistence on my right to object when I considered that the delegation needed some other and contrary point of view. It is, of course, rather lamentable that I should have to say these things in an election year, but since I consider them to be true that must be my justification. As for the members of the department who were at the UN in an advisory or other capacity, I found them always helpful, invariably willing to consider a proposition, frequently overworked, and never ready to say yes when they thought the answer should be no.
Now the whole problem of the secretariat is going to come before the meeting of the United Nations which will start next week. One can only hope that an acceptable solution will be found but as far as acceptability goes I must let the government know that our standards are going to be high. The United Nations is built on twin pillars, one of them being the loyalty of the member states, the other the efficiency, integrity and competence of the men and women who make up the secretariat. We harm the one and we hurt the whole structure; we destroy the one and we bring the structure down around our ears. STet an attempt is being made today, in some quarters innocently, in other quarters with Joe most deadly malice, to destroy the secre-;ariat and the value of the secretariat of the Jnited Nations.
What is Canada's view about the secre-:ariat? We find it expressed in a phrase in his year's copy of "Canada and the United *rations" where it is stated that "a secretariat >f very high calibre has been built up". Che Secretary of State for External Affairs juite understandably said little about this >roblem when he spoke, but I think it would lot be amiss to quote what he said on the !2nd of December on the adjournment of the eventh session of the assembly. He said:
I should like also to take this opportunity of laying a very well deserved tribute to the ecretariat and to its distinguished leader, the ecretary general. The continuity and effectiveness f the general assembly's work must depend very argely on the integrity and efficiency of our inter-[Mr. Stewart (Winnipeg North) .3
national civil servants. The secretariat have once again served us loyally and well, and I should like to express the assembly's appreciation for their extremely hard work and devotion to what is often a thankless and difficult task; and to what is often a misunderstood ideal, that of international service.
Yet if one reads many of the magazines, periodicals and newspapers which come out of the United States one would believe that this organization is riddled with communists, and we are entitled to ask: Who is right? I do not profess to know everything about the secretariat; far from it. But I do know sufficient to say with firm conviction that the belief of Canada in this matter is impeccably right. The secretariat over the last number of months has been the victim of persecution which one can only describe as outrageous. Yet we have to consider it in the light of the whole social scene of the United States. We have to appreciate the intense desire of American parents to bring their own sons home from Korea. We have to appreciate the feeling that perhaps in this United Nations struggle in Korea they are fighting too much alone. It is a position which we in Canada can appreciate, for we remember only too vividly the days of 1939 and of course 1914.
Their anger and their wrath against the communists, when one considers the United States casualties, is understandable, but unhappily it has too often been diverted against the guiltless and innocent. The secretariat of the United Nations has been used as a stick with which to belabour the last administration, and it was so used for many months. There are certain types of politicians in the United States who have found that by crying "communist" loudly enough and often enough they will secure headlines and will be able to bask in publicity. Therefore they have been indiscriminate in their charges and one of the organizations which has suffered most has been the United Nations.
We have of course had the McCarran committee, a group which the Manchester Guardian has described as a grotesque body. We have the grand jury of New York which stated in December that there was infiltration into the United Nations of an overwhelmingly large group of disloyal United States citizens. Is it any wonder then that the people of the United States are afraid and doubtful as to what the United Nations really is doing in that country? Fear and doubt have been spread until the value of the secretariat has substantially diminished. When I was in New York I happened to read a dramatic criticism by Brooks Atkinson of the New York Times. There has been a revival of an old play, The Children's Hour,

and Mr. Atkinson quotes Burns Mantle as having this to say about it in 1934:
The true theme is the curse of scandalmongering and the whispering campaign, the kind of vicious lying that may easily wreck the lives of innocent people.
Mr. Atkinson goes on to say:
We are more keenly aware of the implications of the play today because slander is now a common factor in the life of the nation, accepted by many reputable people as an evil necessary to a search for genuine traitors.
I think Mr. Atkinson was unduly harsh on his own countrymen, for I feel that there are certain hopeful features about the situation, although not in the immediate future. I have a certainty that eventually the Americans will deal faithfully with the calumniators, the traducers of the reputations of men and women working in the secretariat. Yet the problem is an urgent one. I believe that Mr. Atkinson wrote more in anger than in sorrow. That is how I speak. I speak in anger towards a friend who is doing something unworthy and which thereby detracts from the lustre of his own good name.
When the secretariat was formed some years ago it attracted men and women from all countries-men and women who had a sense of devotion and who regarded it as an honour and privilege to work with the organization. They embarked upon their tasks with high hopes and perhaps even higher aspirations. Today those hopes are undermined and those aspirations expiring. The morale of the secretariat is being wantonly destroyed. We permit this to continue at our peril. Permit it to continue and we shall destroy the United Nations. As far as this group is concerned, and I hope other groups in this house, none of us is prepared to be a partner in that project.
Now, what are the duties of the secretariat? Here I quote from the United Nations charter, article 100, subsection 1, which reads in part: In the performance of their duties the secretary general and the staff shall not seek or receive instructions from any government or from any other authority external to the organization.
Subsection 2 reads:
Each member of the United Nations undertakes to respect the exclusively international character of the responsibilities of the secretary general and the staff and not to seek to influence them in the discharge of their responsibilities.
And in article 101, paragraph 3:
The paramount consideration in the employment of the staff and in the determination of the conditions of service shall be the necessity of securing the highest standards of efficiency, competence and integrity.
To go further I have here the rules and regulations of the United Nations secretariat
External Affairs
which were published on December 1 of last year. Regulation 1.1 states that:
Members of the secretariat are international civil servants. Their responsibilities are not national but exclusively international. By accepting appointment, they pledge themselves to discharge their functions and to regulate their conduct with the interests of the United Nations only in view.
Regulation 1, paragraph 3:
In the performance of their duties members of the secretariat shall neither seek nor accept instructions from any government or from any other authority external to the organization.
The position I take is that where a member of the secretariat of the United Nations is loyally fulfilling what is required of him either through the charter or through the staff regulations, then there can be no grounds whatsoever for dismissal, no matter how importunate individual nations may be. Today in the _ United Nations itself many of the ordinarily accepted democratic rights of people have disappeared.
I have in my hand the universal declaration of human rights as adopted by the general assembly of the United Nations on December 10, 1948. Article 12 states:
No one shall be subjected ... to attacks upon his honour and reputation.
That is what is happening today.
Everyone has the right to the protection of the law against such interference or attacks.
That is not happening today. That protection has never been accorded them either by member states or the secretary general whom one would have thought would have gone to the defence of his own staff.
Then one can read also article 19 of this same declaration of human rights:
Everyone has the right to freedom of opinion and expression; this right includes freedom to hold opinions without interference and to seek, receive and impart information and ideas through any media and regardless of frontiers.
Today the degree of fear which prevails m the United Nations is so great that the right to freedom of opinion has disappeared in the sacred name of conformity.
Let me quote again from the grand jury which made its presentment on December 2 of last year-and if one cares to go further one can read the recent report given by the secretary general on January 30, 1953:
This presentment contained no indictments and mentioned no names. It set forth certain conclusions and made certain recommendations. Among the conclusions were statements that there was ''infiltration into the United Nations of an overwhelmingly large group of disloyal United States citizens and that this situation constituted a menace to the security of the United States.
There is the flat assertion that there has been "infiltration into the United Nations of an overwhelmingly large group of disloyal"

External Affairs
people; and yet when one reads this report of the secretary general does one not come appreciably nearer to the facts?
Paragraph 45 of the secretary general's report states:
It should be noted that with a single exception no staff member has ever been indicted or charged in any court with espionage or any other subversive activity. In one case a staff member- not of United States nationality-was convicted of espionage in the United States and left the country. The espionage in no way related to the staff member's functions as a United Nations official. In a further case a staff member-also not of United States nationality-was terminated while on home leave after the United States government said he had attempted espionage.
What then are we to believe, the unsupported testimony of the grand jury which has been accepted as truth by so many or the facts which are given to us by the secretary general himself? Lest there be a feeling that this attack does not affect us as Canadians I may say that feeling is not shared in other quarters and in other nations. The London Times on December 2, 1952, in commenting upon the jurists' report which I shall deal with later, in part said:
It may well not be intended now to pass every international civil servant through the familiar searching sieve of motives, thoughts and associations, as well as deeds, but the menace is there.
As far as I am concerned and as a Canadian, I see this menace in some of these alleged loyalty investigations and I shall be very interested in knowing what stand our government will take if by any unhappy chance a Canadian is ever accused of subversive activity in the United Nations. As far as loyalty tests go, let me quote from a book "The Fear of Freedom", by Francis Biddle, one-time United States attorney general. Mr. Biddle states:
The vice of the federal loyalty program Inheres in Its departure from a basic concept of our laws and constitution that persons should be penalized for their conduct, not for their beliefs, and not for the acts of those with whom they associate.
We in Canada unanimously reject that vice in determining guilt, for thought control is no part of our democratic process. Yet, individuals today are being dismissed because the United States government, without submitting proof, considers them to be subversive. I have here a list of some eleven people and this is the headline in the Winnipeg Free Press "Eleven Communists in UN Pay, U.S. Charges". The article states in part:
The eleven were named in a memorandum made public Thursday over objections of John Hickerson, assistant secretary of state, who cautioned that the state department could have erred by wrongfully naming some persons or by failing to name some who should be named. He emphasized that

none of the adverse reports was based on sworn testimony, and that those named had been given no hearings.
So, because of unsupported testimony, without giving people a chance to defend themselves, we immediately destroy what they depend upon most in this world, their reputation. I am not prepared, because of hearsay, to condemn someone; nor am I prepared to condemn without proof. I think all of us believe that that will not be the standard of our own government, but the unhappy fact is that today the United States is insisting that its national standards shall be carried into the United Nations. There can be no greater danger than to approve of this concept that national standards will decide the fitness of the employees of this organization. I reject that concept completely out of hand, and for a good reason. It was Mr. Justice Black who said that individual freedom and governmental thought probing cannot live together. To us, individual freedom is paramount and that is why we reject these standards.
It is conceivable however that the secretary general, himself under the heaviest influence and pressure, may have accepted them. On several occasions the secretary general has complained that the information which has been given him by the state department is too slight or too scanty to merit the dismissal of an employee. Yet employees have been dismissed. The secretary general states that the only words he has been given are these cryptic words by the state department such as "reject"; "questionable"; and "incomplete". On the basis of these words he has to make up his mind whether or not he defers to the wishes of the United States government. Time after time the secretary general has dismissed employees. The unhappy thing is that when these dismissals were appealed to the administrative tribunal, the highest body of appeal within the United Nations, time after time the tribunal has disagreed with the secretary general and said that there was not sufficient information to warrant the dismissal. However, the secretary general is supreme when it comes to the staff, and he has insisted on his right to dismiss the employee.
The secretary general has had to pay the employees large sums in indemnity for wrongful dismissal. It would be interesting indeed to find out how much has been paid in the way of indemnity for such dismissals. I am not unduly surprised to find that Mr. Lie would like to see the administrative tribunal abolished. A new advisory group has been set up and this may be the precursor to the abolition of the tribunal. But it also

is only advisory. I do not know what its terms of reference are, and I doubt if anybody does. I know that there are two members of this advisory board who are well known to Canadians. The first one is Ralph Bunche and the other is L. W. Brockington. Men such as these, nurtured in our democratic processes, are going to insist that there be evidence before the secretary general dismisses anybody. But if history is a criterion, and I hope in this case it is not, that evidence will not be forthcoming. This advisory group headed by Mr. Brockington, therefore, will be faced with complete stultification. If so, in the near future one can foretell the resignation of the chairman.
The board is going to be faced not only with that problem but with what is called the problem of the host country. Let me say here and now that I am not prepared to concede rights to a host country which are not applicable to every other member nation of the United Nations. Take our own position, for instance. We are a host country to one international organization, the international civil aviation organization in Montreal. Not only are we the hosts, but to some substantial extent we subsidize it. Therefore we could say that, as host country, we ought to have some substantial say in the matter of personnel. On the assumption that the employees are doing their duty as we expect them to do, I wonder what this house would say if it knew that the government had attempted to secure the dismissal of employees in ICAO because the government did not like what they were thinking. I am certain that the row in this house would go beyond all the bounds of propriety.
Yet we are presented with the same argument in the United States. The United States now foots the greatest part of the UN bill, and it is said that we should therefore accede to their desires. That is not an argument which I, for one, am prepared to accept. I have read that a United States senator demanded that what he considered to be subversive elements in the United Nations should be dismissed immediately or the United States would have to consider very carefully whether or not it would continue its large financial appropriation for the purposes of that organization. That, Mr. Speaker, was something too close to blackmail, and I do not like that sort of blackmail. What is going to happen in the United States if the government of that country decides a certain employee is subversive and the government is not prepared to submit evidence to the secretary general, who then states that the employee will not be dismissed?
External Affairs
Here we are faced with the problem as it exists today. I do not know the answer. Possibly the UN could create some new sort of committee to act as intermediary between the secretary general and the state department, a committee which would be supreme and which would finally make the decision on whatever case is presented. Yet I insist that such a decision must be within the terms of the charter, and must be such that no one nation can have the right to interfere with the secretariat itself.
Now, I said earlier that employees had been wrongfully dismissed and their co-workers on the United Nations staff knew that they had been wrongfully dismissed. The latter, therefore, decided to contribute toward a fund for the legal defence of their colleagues. The house might be interested in knowing how this fund was raised, because it was done anonymously. The secretariat of the United Nations did not dare publish a list of contributors, and I doubt if anybody knows who the contributors are. An envelope, with a mimeographed enclosure, was given to every member of the staff. They were asked to contribute, without signing their names and certainly not by cheque, a certain sum of money for the defence of their colleagues. To make sure that none could be accused in this activity all the envelopes had to be returned. When such a situation occurs, I state there is a reign of fear in the secretariat of the United Nations. It is a situation which has to be rectified.
Now, in the midst of this disturbance and conflict, the secretary general decided to appoint three lawyers to answer certain questions. These three lawyers were popularly known as jurists. Again, if I can refer to the London Times, I notice that it scrupulously eschews the use of the word "jurist", and refers to them as lawyers. Nevertheless, I shall defer to the common usage. But, these jurists did this job in about two weeks. In that brief time they resolved questions which had been perplexing other people for months. Their haste, of course, may have been their undoing, because while undoubtedly much of what they say is laudable and there is much with which I can agree, nevertheless, there are some parts of this report which are not acceptable under any circumstances whatever.
The secretary general asked these jurists to deal with the position of United States nationals in the United Nations secretariat. On page 5 of the report the jurists state:
Although your questions relate in terms specifically to United States nationals who are also members of your staff, we have found it impracticable to deal with that subject without taking into account also the position of members of your staff of other nationalities who are resident in the United States . . .

External Affairs
This report, then, covers all members of the secretariat in the United States. On page 19 of their report the jurists proceed to give some advice. I am going to read some of the worst of it, but perhaps in some ways the most important. They say:
In exercising his responsibility for the selection and retention of staff the secretary general should regard it as of the first importance to refrain from engaging or to remove from the staff any person whom he has reasonable grounds for believing to be engaged or to have been engaged, or to be likely to be engaged in any activities regarded as disloyal by the host country.
Let us consider those last words, and I am reading the original report, "activities regarded as disloyal by the host country." In what sort of position would that place a Canadian as far as the United States is concerned? What about a Frenchman or a Belgian or a Norwegian? Surely their loyalties are to their own countries. But we are told that this document deals with all members. If they were loyal to their own countries, automatically they had to be disloyal to the host country. This was nonsense and the phrase was corrected by the three jurists in a corrigendum which was issued later and which read:
Replace the words "any activities regarded as disloyal by the host country" by the words: "any subversive activities against the host country."
Here was the penalty of haste. Let us consider another aspect of this matter. We have men alleged to be international jurists who are setting out terms which govern members of the secretariat of the United Nations. They ask for the dismissal of a person likely to be engaged in subversive activities. But how can Mr. Lie forecast the future? The secretary general is supposed to be a sort of soothsayer; he is supposed to know what is going to happen a couple of years from now. What sort of absurdity is that in terms of law?
Then the jurists go on to suggest that the secretary general should automatically dismiss any employee of the United Nations who pleads the fifth amendment before a United States committee. The fifth amendment to the United States constitution was designed by its framers to be a lamp post to guide the innocent, but today it is a lamp post on which to hang the innocent. That is what the jurists suggest we do.
An individual pleading the fifth amendment before a United States committee such as I have described may do so because of the fear that he may condemn himself out of his own mouth and be subjected to some further criminal action. I believe that there are members of the secretariat who have pleaded the fifth amendment before these committees

for the good reason that they felt that as they were under oath they would be guilty of perjury if they made an error. The questions which were asked are very searching. They went back a long time, even a decade. I doubt if there is any hon. member here who can say what he was doing on June 5, 1942, or with whom he had lunch on that day. Yet if the witness makes a mistake and does not through error, tell the truth, he is guilty of perjury and subject to the full penalties of the law.
There is another aspect to this matter. Some employees found that no matter how guiltless they have been, they were being asked questions, not concerning themselves but concerning their friends, their acquaintances and their colleagues. They had to answer those questions and before they knew what was happening they had woven a web of circumstantial evidence around their own friends. The situation became intolerable. One of the results of such wretched investigations was the death of a distinguished servant of the United Nations, Mr. Abraham Feller. As far as we are concerned, this report cannot and must not be accepted without the most drastic amendment.
There was a letter in the December issue of the Canadian Bar Review signed by W. Friedmann, J. B. Milner and F. E. LaBrie, who are on the teaching staff of the school of law of the University of Toronto, and also by F. R. Scott, of the faculty of law of McGill university. I should like to quote the closing part of this letter which is headed "Loyalty Tests and the United Nations Secretariat." It reads:
The recommendations of the commission, particularly because of the proposed dismissal from employment on grounds of refusal to testify before investigating bodies, have increased the sense of insecurity in the United Nations secretariat. At a time when the United Nations and other international institutions are undergoing severe political testing, the commission's opinion must in all fairness be considered a surprisingly unsatisfactory treatment of the complex problems presented to it. The statute of the International Court of Justice describes as a source of law the "general principles of law recognized among civilized nations". A similar test should determine United Nations standards, of substance as well as procedure. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, approved by the General Assembly in December 1948 by a vote of 48 (including the United States) to 0, with 8 abstentions, also lays down standards which ought at least to be applied to the United Nations itself. The United Nations must work out its own code. Conviction by a national court for such major and generally recognized offences as treason, sedition or the betrayal of official secrets should justify dismissal from the United Nations, but the adoption, in any one country, of special offences, and investigation procedures that fall short of established standards of fairness, cannot be regarded as part of generally recognized principles,

and therefore as a proper standard for the United Nations. Such national practices should not therefore by themselves establish good cause for dismissal.
Within a few days our delegation is going back to the United Nations charged with the high responsibility of maintaining intact the charter of that organization and the inviolable right of the individual in a democracy. We shall watch it with anxiety and also with the hope that it will fulfil these objectives.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to follow my hon. friend in detail, although I realize some of the difficulties incident to the problem that he has brought before the house. I am a believer in the preservation of those things which constitute our freedom. I think all are agreed that we should not allow the United Nations to be weakened by those who would by innuendo and slander destroy the reputation of innocent persons within the secretariat. On the other hand there is the issue to be faced that the security of the state must be assured at all times.
I for one believe that a host country should not adopt measures that would destroy fundamental freedoms; nonetheless, while maintaining the freedoms unimpaired the democracies have the right to demand that diplomatic immunities shall not be utilized as a means to undermine the host state and to provide, for those who practise treason, protection that ought not to be assured to them. Freedom with security must be maintained. I know that we of the British tradition will follow the lead given in the House of Commons in the United Kingdom in the last few days by Sir Douglas Maxwell Fyfe, who, in the course of an address dealing with the serious situation that exists by reason of the changed conditions of modern times and the use by the communists of propaganda to undermine from within the states in which they are living, took his stand for freedom and the preservation of fundamental freedom without which democracy cannot exist.
We have to guard against a very dangerous perversity of human nature, which is that mankind often imitates the thing it hates in order to defeat the subject of its hatred. I shall say no more at this time than that in these days there are tremendous responsibilities on the state to preserve the state from the termites who would destroy it, while at the same time preserving the fundamental freedoms without which democracy cannot survive.
On this occasion I intend to make some general observations in connection with the United Nations assembly, which I had the
External Affairs
honour to attend, and to place before the house some suggestions that have come to me as a result of that privilege and opportunity. It is a privilege, because one sees and hears at first hand what is going on internationally; and it also gives members of the opposition the right and firsthand knowledge to criticize and to offer alternative suggestions without which a discussion on foreign affairs would be as shadowy as it would be meaningless.
As the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) has said, the international situation is a worrying one. Toynbee has described the age in which we live as "a time of troubles." The minister was very optimistic in his word picture of the world situation, and went a long way farther along the road of optimism than did Mr. Churchill a few short days ago upon his return from the United States. The Soviet pendulum seems to swing. Occasionally it looks like impending war, but when resistance and unity are revealed among the democratic nations, the pendulum seems to swing back, and for a time peace seems imminent. At such time for the benefit of the syndicated press Stalin gives an interview indicative of a desire and wish for world peace. But as Tito has said- and he knows the mind of the Soviet- whatever the changed processes may be, the Soviet purpose is still world domination. To use his warning words, "there may be a change in tactics but there is never a basic change in substance."
The reading of history provides lessons for today. Within the last year there was uncovered by the archaeologists of Princeton university in Athens a marble slab which had been carved in 336 B.C., upon which there was an inscription forbidding the establishment of a dictatorship in Athens, and prescribing heavy penalties for anyone who aided or assisted the dictator. And yet within two years after that, Alexander the Great had destroyed the democratic and independent existence of the Athenian republic and the other Greek republics because they had not learned the lesson of unity. They divided into separate units, each of them going its own way and as a result individually fell a prey to dictatorship. That message is a message for today. The free states of 1953 will survive if they stand together and* in uniting for collective security, to use the modern expression, resist the advance of communist dictatorship.
There will always be some who will proclaim the gospel of fear. Whatever stand is taken, dire destruction will follow. We heard the fearful when a stand was taken in Korea

External Affairs
originally in 1950. We hear the fearful again in the situation created by the deneutralization policy of the United States respecting Formosa. We had it when the nations decided to rearm western Germany, or were contemplating steps in that regard. We had it when NATO was set up. On every occasion when the United Nations or the democratic nations have taken a stand, we have been faced with the fear of some that the stand being taken would be provocative to the U.S.S.R. and would lead to war.
Subsequent events have not established the truth of the prophecies that were made by those who fear. That does not mean that I advocate, or that anyone else within the democratic nations advocates, provocative measures; but it does mean that the events of the last few years have clearly established that in strength and in unity there is the only hope for mankind.
An event of the last few days in Europe has been a particularly hopeful one. At ten o'clock in the morning of February 10 an engine pulling 27 cars of German coke crossed the boundary into France without stopping for customs inspection. It was not an operation of smugglers; it was the beginning of a new era in trade in coal, iron and steel in six nations in Europe, some of them hereditary enemies, joined together in a common unity brought about through the dangers incident to the presence of the spectre of communism. That step, Mr. Speaker, no one would have looked forward to in 1945, a step that may ultimately lead to the federation of Europe which was dreamed of during the days of the Council of Vienna. It reveals an unheard of unity in Europe.
These periodic debates on external affairs are very helpful. They clarify the atmosphere. These debates have their value when we find taking part in them men such as the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), who has been engaged for years in international affairs; men of the reputation, capacity and experience of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), whose training in international affairs goes back to 1945; men like the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette), who has spoken with calm authority on this and on other occasions; men like the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) who, following his recent visit to Europe, brings vividly to parliament what he learned there; and I could continue the list.
Now a word on this debate. I was somewhat disappointed not with the quality of language used by the minister in his review, but that in his remarks on this occasion and
those of a few days ago, on February 5, there was no direct information concerning Canada's stand on the question of the deneutralization of Formosa.
A reading of his speech of February 5 reveals qualified acceptance of the new policy of the United States with a veto in the background. There is in his remarks nothing to indicate the stand being taken by the government of Canada on this problem. That is not enough in these days when international problems, with their widespread repercussions, are before us. The uncertainty of the stand to be taken by Canada, and being taken at this time, is not in keeping with Canada's responsibility.
Yesterday the hon. member for Peel made reference in allegorical form to the speech of the minister. I refer to it directly and say that I think it lacked substance when it dealt with the problem of a deneutralized Formosa. In Canada, situated as we are as interpreters between the United States of America and members of the commonwealth, we have to be careful in what we say. We have to refrain from thoughtless criticism of the United States, whose sacrifices and service in Korea for the preservation of the principles for which the United Nations stand are immeasurably greater than the combined activities of the other members of the United Nations. But surely we have a right to more information than that found at page 1639 of Hansard, where the minister said:
The government will follow developments with the closest possible attention and take appropriate action to make our views known if and when the occasion so warrants.
That, I thought, was a weakness in the minister's speech. Great Britain has taken her stand. I am not advocating that stand; but at least we know what the stand is. Canada is in a dual position in that not only are we adjacent to the United States, but the minister now occupies the position of president of the United Nations, a position incidentally equivalent to that occupied by Mr. Dandurand in 1925 in the league of nations.
Then the minister added these words:
Meanwhile I think it would be unwise and premature to jump to dogmatic or critical conclusions concerning the step taken by the United States government, and announced in a statement by President Eisenhower which contained so much that was wise and heartening to us all.
That statement is a masterpiece of circumlocution. It starts off by saying that we are not going to jump to any dogmatic or critical conclusions regarding the policy as to Formosa, but we are heartened by some of the other statements made by the president. I think we deserve a clearer announcement of policy than that.

The situation is a difficult one, and I realize it. All the United Nations are in Korea. All accepted responsibilities when President Truman gave the lead. What is to be done there? What attitude is to be taken? It has been said that there are only three possible attitudes: Fight it out; stick it out; or get out. Yesterday the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) added another alternative to that group.
Fight it out? No, because that is what we are endeavouring to avoid. Stick it out? There is no other course consistent with the preservation of the United Nations for world peace. Get out? That is something beyond the thought of any responsible person in the United Nations. But I do think those three alternatives place the problem before parliament. I realize the tremendous responsibilities resting upon the minister; but I do contend we have a right to know what Canada's position is. Why should not we in Canada know, when people in the United States and in Great Britain know the stand of their governments on this problem? We cannot adopt a mere middle course.
It is of interest that hon. members of the C.C.F. criticize the stand now being taken by the United States. As I recall it, three years ago they criticized the stand taken when Formosa was neutralized. The minister has a responsibility to place this matter before the House of Commons in clear outline. Shall it be a policy that will be merely one of stalemate as the years roll by and the casualties increase? That is one side of the coin. The other is the fearful possibility that any action we take or that is taken by any of the nations within the United Nations may have the result of spreading war not only throughout Asia but throughout the world.
I agree with the minister that this is no time for loose talk; it is no time for cavilling criticism of the United Nations. It is time for unity within the United Nations. In order to have strongly built the foundations upon which the United Nations stand, the world needs a foundation in the hearts and souls of people everywhere. We can have this only when democratic peoples have some conception of the basis for the policies to be taken.
In order to maintain the foundations of the United Nations, and to secure that support, democratic statesmen must place before their people in clear and unequivocal outline something of the stand that the governments of their respective nations intend to take. The great danger, as communism moves across the world, is that our people shall become wearied in well-doing, believing
External Affairs
that all is well and that the shadow of communism will never become a spectre of world destruction.
Last evening in an address over United States radio systems the secretary of state of the United States, Mr. Dulles, drew a dark and fearful picture. His claim was that unless the European nations move promptly toward unity they will risk peril from which it will be beyond American power or world power to save them. He pointed out the need of unity between France and West Germany on the problem of laying the foundations for a continental army. He stated that the only hope for Europe is the European defence community plan which requires the unification of the military forces of France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, The Netherlands and Luxembourg, and he indicated that unless this unity is achieved the North Atlantic Treaty Organization will have the shadow of power but not the substance to meet the threat.
How terrible the problem is. France, realizing that twice in one generation she has been attacked, naturally fears the restoration of a strong German national army. On the other hand, without that army Europe faces communist domination too awful to contemplate. I think Canada could give a lead in this regard by asking the nations who are signatories of this agreement to give France the assurance that Canada will join with Britain in supporting the extension of the NATO charter from 20 years to 50 years so that it will coincide with the period of the European defence treaty. Building hope in Europe is a contribution all in America can make. Show France that we believe in the extension of NATO to the end that if an army, composed in greater or lesser measure of West German forces, is mobilized as part of the European defence army, the principles of NATO will be maintained during the entire period of the European defence period.
I want to come now to the question of the United Nations. In 1945 I had the privilege of being in San Francisco and seeing laid there the foundations of the United Nations, represented as they are today by the doors to the new assembly building which were presented by Canada and depicting truth and brotherhood, justice and peace. In 1945 the minister was one of the architects of that charter, as was the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon). They could not contemplate then the days that lay ahead with communism, operating through its cultists of confusion, endeavouring to undermine and destroy many of the purposes fcr which the United Nations was constituted.

External Affairs
In those days the delegation was composed of representatives of the various parties in the house. Opposition members now are in the position of observers. I think the change was a good and necessary one. I think Canada has given a lead to the members of the United Nations in sending outstanding representatives of the cabinet to the meetings of the general assembly. As everyone knows, Canada has as two of its representatives the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), and in the present assembly the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). Most of the nations, however, are represented by delegates who have not the authority that ministerial rank would give them. Britain has representatives of ministerial rank, as has Canada. I think it would be a great advantage for the United Nations if other nations within the organization would follow the lead given by these two countries.
I am going to review some of the changes that have taken place since the charter was drawn up in 1945 because, as was said yesterday by the hon. member for Peel, with the time coming shortly when the charter is to be subject to review, consideration should be given to recommendations for changes in the charter by the external affairs committee of this house. There is one thing Canada should do, which I think is long overdue, and that is to realize, as the Minister of National Health and Welfare does, the abiding need of the preservation of our fundamental freedoms. Long since there should have been a submission to parliament of the international declaration of human freedoms for approval by parliament and adoption by Canada.
I want to say a personal word about the two ministers. As one who occupied a very ordinary position, I can say that as a result of their kindness and consideration we co-operated in a manner that I will never forget. There was no concealment of information. The observers were allowed to know what was going on. Every possible consideration was shown, thereby assuring an amicable spirit in keeping with the best traditions of Canadian parliamentary life. The Minister of National Health and Welfare made a speech with respect to human rights on the 17th of December in which he said this:
I do not believe it necessary for me to stress here that the question of human rights has become one of primary interest for the United Nations.
He went on to say:
The question of human rights, after all, is the cornerstone of our charter and has been proclaimed all over the world through the universal declaration of human rights.

I would suggest to him that he have the government submit that declaration, now four years overdue, to the parliament of Canada. There can be no justification for the failure of the government to do that. Some might argue that some of the provisions have to do with property and civil rights, but the declaration has no juridical value. It is in effect an embodiment of principles and ideals and it ought to be brought before parliament, for Canada is one of the few nations that, while accepting, proclaiming and practising human freedoms, have failed to show the members of the United Nations that its parliament supports them.
May I here interpolate and say that one of the most interesting events that occurred while I was there was to hear Vishinsky making one of his harangues. I was there as a visitor two years ago when Dr. Vladimir Clementis made his speech and in towering language described the wonders of communism. I was there the day two years later when Vishinsky delivered almost the same speech, and on that very day Clementis was dying on the gallows because he was believed to harbour improper thoughts on the subject of Soviet domination. I will never forget that speech by Vishinsky. I have never known anyone who gave his own autobiography so accurately as he did on that occasion when he was describing, with malicious deviation from the truth, the cruelties which he alleged were perpetrated on the communist prisoners by the United Nations. He said this:
I can hear them shooting down the communists as mad dogs. I see the beating and I hear the shouting. I see the tattooing and I hear that shooting. I hear the rattle of the machine guns and the groans of the dying under their hangmen guards. I see the searchlights, and then I see the end. With their spirits entirely broken they will come quaking with the fear that will have been implanted in them in the course of that procedure; they will be utterly incapable either of asking any questions or . . .
-answering any.
It was a portrait of Vishinsky himself, the author, the perpetrator of the purge of 1938. It was indeed the epitome, those sordid and untruthful words, of all of the tragedy, horror and fearful intensity of communism in practice. That very day the foreign minister of Czechoslovakia went to the gallows, and if I may paraphrase the immortal words of Grey:
The paths of communist glory lead but to the hangman's noose.
Yes, we saw communism that day as it was, from one who knew.
Mr. Speaker, you may ask me what changes in the revision I might suggest? I believe the United Nations assembly is facing

its greatest test today, undermined by those who are its critics. It will meet that challenge if the representatives to the United Nations from its various members give their people a picture of its usefulness. The security council has been emasculated by 55 Soviet vetoes since 1945, but I doubt if the veto power will be changed in any revision that will take place. But the events of the last few years have established and added another veto, not under the charter but a veto of practice and procedure. That veto is in the assembly which, under section 18 of the charter, requires a majority of the members to bring matters before the assembly, and a two-thirds majority in the case of serious matters advanced. In the last few years the assembly is being weakened by small nations joining together and thereby forcing action in placing on the agenda, for consideration by the assembly, matters that have no place on the agenda and are not deserving of consideration, such as those in which the processes of diplomacy have not been exhausted or in respect of which the peace of the world has not been threatened.
I would suggest that it might be possible- and I realize the conditions inherent in the attitude of opposition to change taken by the U.S.S.R. and puppet states that are members -that some tribunal should be set up to determine whether or not any question that is brought up for consideration should be placed on the agenda of the assembly. Unless that is done more and more the assembly will sit for longer and longer periods dealing with matters which have no place on the agenda; matters that were not contemplated by the charter and which have the effect of weakening the power, authority and prestige of the institution upon which the peace of the world depends.
Nations are beginning to take a definite attitude about these matters that are brought before the assembly by the force of the unity of these small nations. They are contending that they are not bound by assembly decisions.
France refused to attend meetings of the assembly when the Tunisian matter was before it. South Africa has declared that under no circumstances will she in any way be bound by the decision of the assembly in connection with apartheid, nor will she recognize any commission set up by the United Nations to be sent to investigate the problem.
Mr. Speaker, whenever the nations within the United Nations refuse to recognize the authority of the acts or decisions of the
External Affairs
assembly, a destructive influence follows that will literally weaken the institution itself.
There is another effect. The bringing up of these problems of colonialism and nationalism have the effect of providing the U.S.S.R. and its puppets with a trumpet stand for world-wide propaganda designed to separate, designed to unnerve the determination of the members of the United Nations, to arouse antagonism and create sores of hatred all over the world. When the question of revision of the charter is discussed, these are some of the matters that deserve consideration.
I could go on and refer to various other matters but on this occasion I am not going to do so. What I have in mind is simply that in the revision if it is at all possible these influences and tendencies that are causing fissures to appear in the structure of the United Nations must be removed; otherwise the United Nations, with a very proud record to date in the settlement of international disputes by bringing together nations that are in disagreement and by affording opportunity for negotiation, will be weakened in its power for good and will lose much of the prestige it now possesses.
As I listened to the delegates of these various members of the United Nations I thought of the changed world that we are passing through. Colonialism is over; nationalism is on the march everywhere in the world. Above everything else members of the coloured races are demanding that we of the democratic nations no longer practise discrimination against them. How few realize that in the commonwealth five out of every six are of a coloured race. The commonwealth permits of this because of justice and the practice of non-discrimination. The United Nations with its great crusade on behalf of the preservation of peace will succeed if communism is denied its mission of aggression everywhere in the world.
I conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying this. The United Nations must be supported as never before. Undermining it by criticism that is unfounded will destroy that only agency that can preserve peace. Human freedoms everywhere must be upheld and maintained. Discrimination against colour or race, wherever it exists, must be ended, and the great agencies of the United Nations that would help the unfortunate everywhere in the world must be supported. Poverty, if not banished, is a fertile field for the incubation of communism.
While these ideals are being achieved we must, at all costs, regardless of where we

External Affairs
sit in this house, uphold whatever government is in power in maintaining our defences and in assuring unity between the various nations within the United Nations, without which the future of mankind will be dark and fearful.
