speechtext:
It is a matter of pride to all Canadians that our representation at the United Nations has been of such an able and outstanding character. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) is a model of patience, and I think that in dealing with the philosophers from Asia and Europe he has been able to remain calm and not lose patience when interpreting the wish of the Canadian people for peace in the world-not at any cost, but that certainly is our great objective. The world will long remember the work of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) of this country and his able minister of external affairs in dealing with international problems at a critical time in the history of the world.
It is fitting that I should have a few words to say here this afternoon, because the riding which I represent is closer in air miles to the scene of conflict than possibly any other riding in Canada. We see airplanes leaving Fort Nelson and other airports daily. We realize we are only a matter of hours from the shores of Asia. In British Columbia we realize that we are in a great era of Pacific development. The Pacific ocean means more to us than it does to Canadians who are farther inland. We are more deeply touched by the news which comes to us from time to time from across the Pacific.
I am one of those who believe that in international affairs we must do a good job of the work at home. I feel there are certain things that we can do in the northwest which would be of great military advantage, and would also be of advantage to the civilan population of this dominion. I believe that the extension of highways and railways into these fertile valleys is one such thing. I believe that the placing of new populations in these valleys on the northwestern frontier of this Canada of ours would make a contribution to the military defence of this continent.
North of Edmonton at the present time there is a sort of Maginot line because of the lack of adequate transportation. In the event of an attack upon this continent we would be sadly handicapped because of the lack of railway communication with the territory of Alaska, which is the great defence perimeter on this North American continent. In saying that I am only repeating what I have said before in this house, and repeating the words of outstanding military men, particularly in the United States. I believe that

if the record were examined you would find that General Eisenhower himself, prior to taking over his political responsibilities in the United States, was one of those who advocated the construction of a railway to Alaska for the defence of this continent.
I say, therefore, that one way, and not too expensive a way, of helping out today would be to move people into these valleys. We have heard of the catastrophe in Holland. It is unfortunate that a disaster of that kind should occur before we become impressed with our opportunity and also the need of putting people from these congested countries into the vacant valleys in the northwestern part of this land.
So far as the Korean situation is concerned, I may say that I have listened carefully to the speeches and the various opinions that have been expressed. I was bound to look up a little verse written by James Russell Lowell about a hundred years ago in the Bigelow Papers, which pretty well sums up what a lot of statesmen and public men are saying today about Korea. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I shall quote this verse:
Ez for war, I go agin it,-[DOT]
I mean to say, I kind o' du,
Thet is, I mean, that bein' in it,
The best way was to see it thru;
Not but whut abstract war is horrid I sign to that with all my heart,-
But cilyzation does get forrid,-
Sometimes upon a powder cart.
Korea has been a school for the training of warriors. There is no doubt about that. I often wonder if some of our Chinese friends are not obtaining education in the arts of modern war at the expense of some of the western nations. I am afraid that the nationalist army, when it is released and allowed to leave Formosa for the mainland of China, will simply melt into the great Chinese army.
I do not set myself up as an expert on these matters, but having had dealings with the Chinese, I see a danger in the acceptance of the opinion of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) that we should blockade the Chinese coast. I think the proposition of blockading the Chinese coast is something that we should not consider at this time. I believe that the containment of the war in Korea has been a tremendous achievement.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we Canadians have the opportunity to establish ourselves in the hearts of the countries of Asia, and this is well illustrated by the Colombo plan. We are a young country and our hands are clean so far as international politics are concerned. We have done nothing in China other than help the Chinese, and so it is in all the countries of Asia.
The efforts of the Christian missions of Canada in Asia makes the brightest chapter in the history of that ancient continent. In Formosa, of which we have heard so much today, the pioneer missionary during the last century was a Canadian from the county of Oxford, Dr. G. L. MacKay. He built and equipped a college there, which he called Oxford College after the county of Oxford, to train medical men, nurses and others to minister to the health and welfare of those people. He was one of the many Canadians who have operated in the mission field in the Far East.
I suggest to men who are wealthier than I that they consider endowing universities in Canada so that studies by Asiatic pupils in Canada may be extended. Funds might also be set aside to make it possible for Canadian young men and women to visit Asiatic lands and study at first hand the languages and customs, conditions and cultures of those peoples. It is not to the credit of Canada that we had to leave the task of visiting Asia and going about among the

External Affairs
people there in 1952 to such men as a certain communist leader from Toronto. I feel that those who have a positive contribution to make, such as students, leaders, political personalities and others, might well forgo the field of Europe for a while and make a close study of conditions on the other side of the Pacific.
What has happened in the Far East is that the native people have learned too quickly from the white man. China has her broadcasting systems today and television is operating in Japan. Radio broadcasting has been operating in continental China for the last 30 years. China has a network of airfields. Her civilian aviation Was growing when world war II interfered. Chinese aviators are keen flyers, as many of you know. In the world of aviation they have proved their great ability.
China has been steadily developing her industries and is increasing her manufactures of iron and steel products, textiles, chemicals and ships. Japan planned to be her manufacturing centre and to exploit her, but the Chinese are rapidly becoming skilled in all lines of manufacture. That country uses Russian machine guns, but makes a lot of her own. China needs mineral development, better roads, more docks and wharves, hydroelectric services and railways. It is said that there are 10,000 cities in China today that need public utilities, including hydroelectric service. She needs grain elevators, ships and locomotives.

speechtext:
And she needs the friendly help of the nations of the rest of the world. Her position with regard to Russia is that of a nation in great extremity, and she is compelled to call upon Russia. If we were to blockade the ports of China we would weld that country into the structure of the Soviet empire. She would be compelled to do that because by shutting her out from ocean trading we would force her to trade within her own country, which has 3,000 miles or more of frontier with Soviet Russia, just as we have a very large boundary line with the United States, If Canada were blockaded on the Atlantic and Pacific we would be compelled to turn to the nearest nation to make purchases and carry on our activities. Therefore if we were so rash as to blockade the ports of China we would undoubtedly contribute to an international situation which would not be cleared up in our time.

History itself shows the futility of trying to do anything about blockading the ports of China. Since 1842 Britain and her associates have had control of certain ports in China. They had extraterritorial rights in all the great cities. They had virtual control of all the trade that went into China from the Pacific ocean; yet at the end of it all we had the humiliating experience of being drummed out of Shanghai, Canton, Hanoi and other great ports and were forced to give way so that any effort at coercion or to rule by force along the coast of China I am afraid will not meet with any greater success in this century than it did in the last.
You who know the Chinese people realize that they are a people with a history reaching back 40 centuries or more. I have read a translation of a book on farming which referred to records of 40 centuries of farming in China. Arnold Toynbee, the historian, says that they will survive any war, any shock. He say that they are a spiritual people, and that if he could return to this earth a good many generations hence he would expect to find the Chinese still placidly going about their affairs. He also mentions one other nation that would probably survive over the next five hundred years, namely Canadians, and particularly the Canadians of the province of Quebec. But he is not so hopeful of other groups. He says the Chinese and the Canadians have their roots deep in the soil and they love their land. They have spiritual values which they have always placed far above mere material things.
I do not propose to go into a long digression upon that ancient empire, with its 500 million and more people, but I would like to take this opportunity to refer to the great work of William Lyon Mackenzie King, who as a young man was sent to Asia by Sir Wilfrid Laurier. It was wise Sir Wilfrid Laurier who dispatched Mr. King to Asia at the turn of the century and instructed him to do all he could to work with delegates of other countries towards the suppression of the international opium traffic. It was a mission crowned with success. The delegates met at Shanghai, Peking and Tokyo, and began an international movement to outlaw opium and the traffic in narcotic drugs of all kinds. In those days Mr. King, almost a beardless boy, who had a talent for observation and inquiry, was exposed, as I say, to the impact of the Far East. I should say his journey was of historic importance, because through the long years of his career we find him appearing and reappearing at the council tables of the nations where the affairs of Asia were s*/i-ously discussed.

The United States of America was never a member of the league of nations, but the records show that the U.S.A. supplied almost unlimited funds to assist the league of nations in stamping out the opium traffic, and here again we had Mr. King counselling the leaders of the world. It might well be said that the league of nations justified its existence by the work it carried out with respect to outlawing narcotic drugs, a work in which Russia, China, Japan and India co-operated to the full.
I was going to pay some attention to the trade opportunities which exist on the coast of British Columbia with respect to the development of the Chinese and other Pacific markets, but time does not permit. I would take this opportunity to pay a compliment to the new minister who has been appointed to Japan, an industrialist from the city of Victoria, a former minister of fisheries in this government. I am sure that in his position over there he will do a great deal toward the development of further trade relations between the countries of Asia, despite war and rumours of war, and the west coast of Canada.
The work of the United Nations in saving us from a world-wide conflagration is something we cannot praise too highly. When we think of that country over there with its vast population and its huge armies, we realize that the cost of the revolution which took place within the last ten or fifteen years, the cost of the operation in Korea today, is astounding. The cost of a day's operations there would build great modern hospitals, in half a dozen towns in China. The cost of our own United Nations troops would build an equal number of hospitals. The costs of a single day would clear away slums in that great country where millions of natives live in filth and squalor. It would irrigate thousands of acres of land in Asia, not now being cultivated, to feed their starving populations. It would build dams for hydroelectric development, the development of natural resources. The money used for war would, if turned to peaceful purposes, change the whole face of Asia.
I repeat that some of us feel that we are competent to advise on these new international things. Certainly when one judges by some of the speeches he has heard we have here certain men who have very radical ideas on what should be done. An old philosopher said that China is a rug, the rest of the world but a fringe of the rug. I remind you that China is bigger than Europe; that it has, as I have said, more than 3,000 miles of coast line.
If we were to blockade the ports of China we would also have to blockade the ports
External Affairs
of Siberia. What would be the point in blockading the ports of China if the great port of Vladivostok and other places in the north which lead into Soviet Russia were left open? It would take the United States, the Canadian and the British navies combined to enforce the blockade. As I say, we would back Chinese trade into the interior and force them to get in deeper with Russia, in closer harmony with Russia, whose boundary for more than 3,000 miles is common with that of China. A blockade would mean all-out war, and I would object to sending boys from the Peace river to travel over to China to engage in such a war, to take them from peaceful occupations and throw them into the holocaust of an all-out war on the continent of Asia.
There must be some other way, Mr. Speaker, and I think that way is being found by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, by the Prime Minister of this country and by the various leaders who have spoken in this debate, so that somehow, somewhere, we shall appeal to the hearts of these people and win them to the paths of peace.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we of the C.C.F. group agree with those who have said that at this juncture in world affairs the views of the various groups in this house should be stated quite clearly. Hon. members will recognize that that was most certainly done on our behalf yesterday by my colleague the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis).
Meantime, however, there have been expressions of views by other members and other groups in the house which make it seem necessary to us to give at least some restatement of the definite position taken on our behalf yesterday. In that connection let me say that we find ourselves in agreement with a good deal of what has just been said by the hon. member who has just taken his seat. I shall come in a moment or two to a discussion of some of the points on which he has spoken.
We feel that our fundamental aim in Canadian foreign policy at this time should be to end and not to extend the war in Asia. It is because of that fundamental conviction that we have taken our stand with respect to a number of specific matters.
In our view there is no point in trying to oversimplify the case as some hon. members have done during the course of this debate. From a debating standpoint it may be easy to say, as some members have said, that the west should deal with this situation in the same way the communists are dealing with it. It is very easy to say, as some members are saying, that if we do not blockade the

External Affairs
China coast, that means we are permitting materials of war to reach that country to be used against our troops fighting in Korea. It is very easy to say that because the other side is doing so-and-so it is perfectly logical and justifiable for us to follow the same course.
As I have already indicated, you cannot oversimplify the international situation in that way. There are risks either way. One has to weigh the risks. One has to determine what is the basic aim. And in our view- and we believe the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) agrees with us in this-the basic aim at the present time should be to end and not to extend the war in Asia. Through all of this we must make sure that our stand is firmly on the side of freedom; but let us not go along with the kind of mistakes that might involve us in the holocaust of a third world war, and the end of freedom itself.
It is because of that basic belief that it should be our aim at the present time to see the end rather than the extension of the war in Korea, that we are critical of the stand taken by the new administration in the United States. We refer in particular to the order given by President Eisenhower to change the order with respect to the operations of the seventh fleet between Formosa and the mainland of China. And, as I shall show in a few moments, we feel that we should be deeply concerned, lest that first item in the new United States foreign policy in the Par East be followed by other items which could lead us down the path to a third world war.
As I have already said, we believe that the government, indeed the Secretary of State for External Affairs, shares our views in this connection, despite some of the things said in this debate and despite editorials such as the one that appeared a day or so ago in the Ottawa Journal. But our quarrel with the minister is that, though you can find in his speech of Wednesday and in his statement of a week ago yesterday the position we believe he takes, you have to hunt for it with a fine-tooth comb. We think he should take a lesson from the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray), who has just taken his seat, and express his views as well as the views of the government much more clearly than he has done thus far.
A week ago yesterday, as recorded at page 1639 of Hansard the minister did say-and he put it a little more strongly then than he did in his speech on Wednesday-
With respect to the position of the Canadian government, while we remain resolved to carry out our United Nations obligations in Korea, we do not 
think that the defence of Formosa, which has not been assumed by the United Nations, should be confused with the defence of Korea, which has.
That, we suggest, is an implied criticism of the action of President Eisenhower, for that action in our view does confuse the defence of Formosa-indeed it confuses the whole question of the Chinese civil war- with the defence of South Korea, which is our chief concern in that part of the Far East at the present time.
Despite that statement on February 5 which some of us thought might be a prelude to a stronger statement when he made his more extended remarks in the course of this debate, when that time arrived the minister used even more cryptic language. Nevertheless, while I am critical of the minister for not making his statement clearer and more definite, at the same time I give him credit for having said what he did say, and for holding the views which these sentences imply. So I should like to put them on the record again, as they appear in Hansard of February 11 at page 1852. This is what was said by the Secretary of State for External Affairs on that occasion:
As I said a few moments ago the most recent attempt at the United Nations general assembly to end the war in Korea has failed. But the effort to that end must not stop, and I am sure it will not stop. The guiding principle of Canadian policy in Korea is to continue to do everything possible to limit the present hostilities to the Korean peninsula, and to take advantage of any opportunity for an early settlement of these hostilities by peaceful negotiation. It follows from this that our general attitude in the United Nations general assembly, as elsewhere, is to support proposals designed to facilitate an armistice agreement, and to oppose proposals which, in our judgment, would impede such an armistice.
As I have already said, we agree with that statement. We agree with what is implied; but we feel-and in a moment or so I shall develop our reasons for feeling this way- that the minister should have said it much more openly, and that he should have put it in the forefront of his speech, rather than bury it in the middle, as he did.
Then after another paragraph he said this:
We consider also that the purpose of the United Nations in Korea remains the defeat of aggression, there, and does not include intervention in the civil war in China. So long as Chinese troops act as aggressors in Korea they must be opposed and that aggression, if possible, defeated. This does not mean that we who oppose them, by so doing, are committed to the overthrow by force of the government now in effective control of the mainland of China. As we see it we are engaged not in a national war against communist China or in intervening in a Chinese civil war, but as a member of the United Nations in a police action against aggression.
I say again, Mr. Speaker, that we agree with those sentiments. We feel that they

should be made to stand out, that the minister should have put them in more clear-cut language, and that his remarks on behalf of the Canadian people, for whom he speaks in matters of foreign policy, should have been directed clearly to our friend and neighbour, our ally, the great country to the south of us. The reason we are anxious that that be done, despite all the rules and practices of diplomacy, is that we very much fear that if this government, in the name of the Canadian people, offers no strong criticism of this first step that the new United States administration has taken, it will be that much more difficult to offer criticism of a second step. So we will go on down the line until we find ourselves involved in a succession of agreements to successive steps, the fourth or fifth one of which may be the step that leads us into the catastrophe of a third world war.
There is no doubt in my mind from what the minister has said that he disagrees with a policy the apparent aim of which is to take action with respect to something other than the Korean war, in this case the Chinese civil war. But despite the obvious opposition that the minister feels to what President Eisenhower has done, he covers that opposition by saying, as he did on an earlier occasion, that he trusts President Eisenhower's non-aggressive intentions. Well, I suggest that that is giving to President Eisenhower, and perhaps what is more important and more ominous, to those around him who help to shape United States foreign policy, the notion that if they take another step, a step such as the hon. member for Cariboo has just been objecting to-the proposal to blockade the China coast-or if they decide to bomb communist bases in Manchuria, somehow or other Canadians will still trust President Eisenhower's non-aggressive intentions. That will not be so, and therefore it seems to me that the time to speak out and say to our friends in the United States in friendly but firm terms that we disagree with the course upon which they are embarking is now, at the time of the very first step.
The positions of the various parties in the house on this question now seem to have been made clear. There have been doubts in the minds of some members as to where the government stood. I thought the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) was trying yesterday Ho pull the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) into bed with him, but I hope I have got him out of that bed by putting on Hansard the quotations I have just read from the minister's previous statements. It is clear-and the members of
External Affairs
these groups are here to correct me if I misinterpret them-that both the Progressive Conservative and the Social Credit parties support and go along with what they call the stiffening policy being adopted by the new administration at Washington. At least they are stating clearly where they stand, and that is the duty of each group in this house.

speechtext:
No. I think I made it clear that the only statement or change of policy that I have attributed directly to President Eisenhower himself, in my remarks today, is the change with respect to the seventh fleet. I said that the other statements that were being made, suggesting the blockading of the China coast or the bombing of the bases in Manchuria, were coming from others in congress and from military leaders in various parts of the United States. Of necessity President Eisenhower must get advice, must have people around him to help formulate policy, and my fear is that if unchecked by the voice of people on this North American continent who are friendly to the United States they might go on down the path that can lead to the third world war that we all hope can be prevented.
I want to say that in our view it is not only in the Far East that we feel the new administration is making certain mistakes. We feel that this is also happening in respect of the situation in Europe. Consequently we believe that there too the voice of Canada should be heard, in friendly but firm terms, in order to help the United States administration get on a more hopeful and helpful pathway.
It has often been said that Canada's position in world affairs is to a large extent that of an interpreter between the United States and western Europe in particular, as well as between the United States and the countries that make up our commonwealth. There is no denying the fact of that situation, and it is one indeed of great importance. It is our view that at this particular juncture it is extremely important that we try to interpret to the United States, and in particular to the new administration at Washington, what we feel to be a proper understanding with respect to the situation in western Europe and also with respect to 
the commonwealth of nations to which we belong. In that connection it does seem to us that the new administration, through its secretary of state, Mr. Dulles, is showing a lack of understanding of the situation in western Europe. That lack of understanding, I submit, has been portrayed by some of the statements Mr. Dulles made both before his recent trip to Europe and while he was over there, not to mention some of the statements he has made since he came back.
Hon. members are generally familiar with the statement that Mr. Dulles made late in January over television, the full text of which was printed in the New York Times of Wednesday, January 28, 1953. I refer in particular to this paragraph:
The United States has made a big investment in western Europe on the theory that there could be unity there. Of the $40 billion which we have sent abroad since the end of the second world war, almost $30 billion have gone into western Europe. If however, there were no chance, and that I just refuse to believe, but if it appeared there were no chance of getting effective unity, and if in particular France, Germany and England-
Perhaps I might be permitted to pause here and say, along with others who have quoted this, that I suppose Mr. Dulles meant the United Kingdom.
-should go their separate ways then certainly it would be necessary to give a little rethinking to America's own foreign policy in relation to western Europe.
We have assumed for the last number of years that the United States was in with the countries of western Europe in the terms of a partnership. We have recognized that the role of the United Stateis has had to be that of one with greater wealth to share in such a way as to assist some of the other members of that partnership. Still, we have thought of it as a partnership, and it seems to me that we owe a considerable debt of gratitude to people like Roosevelt and Truman for their part in helping to bring an end to the isolationist sentiment that was common in the United States for so long.
Having mentioned the names of those two former presidents of the United States, I must say that I was shocked yesterday and deeply disappointed to hear the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) refer to the late Franklin Roosevelt and to Mr. Harry Truman, now of Independence, Missouri, as the betrayers of humanity, or the betrayers of mankind.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: REFERENCE OF ESTIMATES OF DEPARTMENT TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I take it, from the approval with which my remarks in that connection are now greeted, that this house generally does not share that view at all.

I was on the point of saying that it was through what those two men did, along with their other contributions to the good of mankind, that the United States did seem to get pulled out of its isolationist approach, and its people in our view seemed to become partners in the common effort to find a means to get away from war, in the hope that we might yet build a world of peace and human accord.
When one member of that partnership, even if it is the member that has had to shell out dollars-and do not forget that some of the other members shelled out something more precious than dollars-starts to threaten other members, threatening to withdraw its dollars and its support unless other members follow a course dictated by that partner, then the situation is, I would suggest, fraught with real difficulty.
My feeling about this matter is not that we should fly off the handle and holler about it; nevertheless we should speak pretty plainly out of the role we occupy as an interpreter between the United States on the one hand, and Britain and the commonwealth on the other. As we play that role of interpreter we should try to get our friends in Washington to see the difficulties that will flow from their following that sort of course.
As hon. members know, after making this statement on television which I have just quoted, Mr. Dulles went over to Europe and travelled around. He visited a number of the countries there and it appears from quite a few press reports that he gave what amounted to an ultimatum, namely that the countries of western Europe should get together and achieve unity along the pattern in the mind of the United States within seventy-five days, or else. For example, here is a story as it appeared in a dispatch by Raymond Daniell, dated February 4, to the New York Times which appeared in that paper on February 5:
According to foreign diplomats the line that Mr. Dulles has taken everywhere on his European trip is that Congress has reached the limit of its patience and wants action . . .
Later on he said:
Unless there is action on the part of European legislators or a definite promise of it within 75 days he will find it very difficult to convince Congress that further appropriations should be made for Europe's defence.
As I say, there are a number of news dispatches on that point but they are all in the same vein and it appears that since Mr. Dulles returned to this continent, even in a speech made last night, he is still expressing the view of the United States that Europe must unite, or else. He put a little different
External Affairs
twist on it last night because, if my memory serves me correctly from a reading of the papers this morning, he said that unless Europe were to unite soon nothing the United States could do could save that part of the world.
Now, when you hear things like that, with the background of the opposition that was expressed by some of the leading Republicans to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, and when you remember the statement of Senator Robert Taft that this would be a case of rearming western Europe at American expense, one sees in the statements of Mr. Dulles what may well be an attempt to condition the American people to the idea of lessening the responsibility of the United States for the defence of freedom in the western part of Europe.
On the one hand we have this great neighbour of ours doing things in the Far East which we think are provocative, unnecessarily provocative, and in danger of bringing on a third world war. On the other hand in Europe you have this neutralist attitude, this pulling out, this saying to the countries of western Europe that unless you get together and do things the way we say they should be done, well, we just cannot sell the idea to the American people any longer.
Mr. Speaker, all of this beclouds the question as to what are the purposes and interests of the United States in western Europe. I believe that it will be far better if western Europe can unite and federate. There is no question but that a good deal of the trouble we have had across the years has been because of the division of that relatively small continent into so many different units. But for the United States to say to those countries that they must achieve unity in the European defence community or unity on whatever pattern the United States lays down, or be denied United States help is, I submit, the wrong way to go about it.
Several members in the debate have already referred to the significance of that train that crossed the boundary from Germany to France at one o'clock the other morning without having to stop for any customs inspection. Surely that six-nation Schuman plan is a step in the right direction, something for which we are all extremely grateful. It holds great promise for the future. But is not the situation this, that it is far better to encourage these countries to go on with this kind of thing rather than submit them to the kind of threat that Mr. Dulles has been handing out?
Now, what is our part in all this, Mr. Speaker? I come back again to the statement that is so often made, namely that we

External Affairs
are in the position of being the interpreter between these two parts of the world. The United States is closer to us than it is to Europe. As a matter of fact, if I may inject a personal note, I see over there my good friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) and my good friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) both of whom, like myself, were born in the United States. We had the good sense and good fortune to come to this country as soon as we could, and I had the good fortune to be born of Canadian parents. At any rate, there are many of us in this country who have the kind of connection with the United States that makes our relationship that of friends who surely can speak to each other quite clearly and plainly.
I contend that our government's spokesman on foreign policy, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), should talk plainly to the United States, both publicly and privately if he has a chance to see Mr. Dulles, and try to interpret to him the position of these other parts of the world, Britain and western Europe, with which we in this country have such a close connection.
Part of this whole problem as it arises at the present time lies in the age-long suspicion, if I may call it that, that exists between Germany and France. Right now there is a desire in many quarters that the European defence community be completely ratified. Hon. members know that in these countries, particularly in Germany and France, a great many reservations are being made and there are a great many stumbling blocks to the possibility of complete ratification of the protocol between the European defence community and NATO. As a matter of fact, as one looks over the reservations of each of these countries-they are some ten or twelve in number for one and six or seven for the other-one cannot help but sympathize with some of these reservations. I think the position of these countries should be interpreted to the United States. They should be told, in the meantime, not to go around handing out these 75-day threats, and supposing that as a result of that kind of threat immediate action will be taken.
As a matter of fact, the ominous feature of this whole business is that at the present time the picture in regard to western European unity is not as bright as it was before Mr. Dulles started making these television pronouncements and these threats in various parts of the world. It is not my privilege to talk to Mr. Dulles, but it may be the privilege of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Certainly when he speaks in
fMr. Knowles.]
this house on foreign policy he speaks even more than the rest of us for Canada. I think he should speak plainly as a Canadian friend to our United States friends on this whole question.
There is something else in what Mr. Dulles has been saying. I refer to that passage where he mentioned England and where we presumed he meant the United Kingdom. He objected to that country going its own way, rather than doing the bidding of the United States. There is something there that it seems to me Mr. Dulles and others do not fully appreciate, and that is the peculiar relationship between Britain and the countries of the commonwealth. That is one of the problems that Britain faces in tying up with the proposed military set-up on the continent of Europe. The United Kingdom forever has to keep in mind its relations with the commonwealth countries, particularly the Asian members of the commonwealth.
I suggest that even if Britain did not want to remember that connection for her own sake, we want her to remember the connection with the Asian members of the commonwealth for the sake of the peace of the world as a whole. In my view it is one of the fortunate elements in the picture at the present time, in view of the danger of conflict between the east and the west, conflict on a racial or a colour basis, that wo have this association of nations, free and voluntary as it is, known as the commonwealth, including the great countries of India, Pakistan and Ceylon, along with the rest of us in this world-wide association. One wonders whether the importance of the commonwealth in holding our world together is fully appreciated by the people in Washington.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I see that it is just about six o'clock. Although I have a few more minutes remaining I shall not use them. I am prepared to conclude my remarks at this time. I hope that, like my colleague the member for Vancouver East, I have made it clear that we believe Canada should stand very clearly on the side of freedom. We believe also that the facts of the situation require that we assess the risks involved in going one way or the other, that we calculate the risks that confront us at the present time. We believe that, having done that, we must do our best to avoid the pursuit of any policy that would lead to the extension rather than the ending of the war in Asia. We feel we must avoid any course that would break down the larger unity that has been built up in the North Atlantic

community and in western Europe, within the framework of the United Nations.
Because we take that position we feel that our voice should be one of strong and friendly advice to the United States. In other words, we have no quarrel with what the minister said in terms of foreign policy when you have read his speech closely enough to find it. The trouble is that the important points were buried in the middle of his speech and covered up with words that seemed to be chosen so that they would not be seen by the new administration in the United States. We think it should be said clearly to that country that we recognize the important part they are playing in the leadership of the free world. We recognize the importance of our friendly relations with them. But as my colleague said yesterday, we think we should not just be told what is being done; we should be consulted and in that consultation we should advise the administration at Washington that we believe no steps should be taken at this time that could lead to an extension of the war in Asia. Our immediate aim should be to bring to an end as soon as possible the present conflict in Korea. Having done that we should go on and do our best to pursue a course that will enable us to achieve permanent peace for all mankind.

May I call it six o'clock?
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, the importance of foreign affairs to Canada is so great that I am venturing to participate in this debate. I think it is only by a full discussion that we can arrive at the desired unified policy.
We are engaged in what appears to be a very serious struggle with the forces of communism. So far that struggle has not become one of global war with the navies, armies and air fleets of the world locked in mortal combat. It is possible that it will not be extended to a world-wide war. The strategy of the communist powers appears to take the form of a long-term process of erosion, with force applied here and there on the perimeter and psychological warfare increasingly pressed throughout the world.
Russia, unified and controlled by a military oligarchy, in some respects has an advantage over the freedom-loving democracies whose military alliances are subject to all the stresses and strains that must be expected if 68108-123J
External Affairs
freedom to express opinions and to disagree is to be maintained; and without that freedom democracy would have no meaning.
With those thoughts in mind I suggest___
and I am merely restating what others have already put forward-that we base our policy upon the premise that communism constitutes an external and internal threat to the democratic nations of the world, that that threat may well continue for a very long time, and that it can be met only by preparedness and eternal vigilance.
We should recognize the fact that a serious and perhaps decisive war for freedom is being waged in Asia; that the democracies must be fully prepared to resist any communist threats in Europe and the Middle East, and that an all-out effort must be made to perfect our military defences so that neither surprise nor superior forces will achieve success against us.
In my opinion the first thing to do is to create a proper climate of opinion. We should drop the terms "cold war" and "police action". We should avoid being misled in the future by insincere suggestions of an armistice in Korea. We should recognize that there is no immediate possibility of terminating the Korean war. We should generally settle down to a determined long pull against the communist menace.
We are faced by a crafty and implacable enemy who now controls one-third of the earth surface and 800 million people; an enemy who is practically self-sufficient in all materials necessary for war except oil; an enemy who appears to be planning or plotting the destruction of the western democracies, and who desires domination of the world. In his speech of January 27, as printed in U.S. News and World Report of February 6, Mr. Dulles used these words:
-me tnreat is
