Eisenhower recently said this nation stands in greater peril than at any time in our history Any American who isn't awake to that fact is like a soldier who s asleep at his post. We must be awake, all of us awake, to that danger.
If the United States is in greater peril than at any time in its history, so is Canada- for our fortunes are inextricably linked 'with those of our neighbour to the south upon whose shoulders rests now the grievous weight of world leadership. Canadians must be just as awake to the peril as Americans-but if we continue to talk about the "cold war" and "police action", and use the term "cold peace" recently foisted upon a quiet, peaceful and unsuspecting public by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) if press reports are accurate, we shall certainly obscure the issue and run the risk of adopting an attitude of complacency.

External Affairs
Hon. members will recall the period in 1939, alter the fall of Poland, to May 1940. That period was dubbed by careless observers "the phony war", and a go-slow and complacent attitude was adopted. It was not until the cataclysm struck in May 1940, and again in December, 1941, that the world was awakened to the gravity of the situation. Let us not make the same mistake again.
We are obviously engaged in a major war in Asia. It is unfortunate that the war is not viewed in the proper light as a war on three fronts, Korea with the threat to Japan, Indo-China and Malaya with the threat to southeast Asia, the rice bowl of the Far East. The forces on both sides comprise at least three million armed men. Casualties have reached a large total. It is war on a very considerable scale, and far from being limited in scope, it shows every sign of increasing in intensity and of becoming spread more widely as the nationalist forces of Chiang Kai-shek once again enter the conflict.
During the past year and a half we have been misled by the armistice negotiations in Korea into thinking that that particular phase of the warfare in Asia could be brought to an end. Surely it is obvious now that the communist powers never had any sincere desire to bring to a conclusion the war in Korea. The armistice talks were used as a cover for an intensive build-up of the Chinese army and for an intensive program of fortification and consolidation. At the same time the psychological effect of the negotiations served the purpose of lulling the United Nations into a mood of complacency.
There is now a widespread feeling that a full-scale effort on the part of the United Nations might bring the war in Korea to an end. I might point out that there is some difference of opinion among experts with regard to that. Nevertheless there has been considerable talk about bringing to an end the war in Korea, as if that would end the struggle against communism.
I notice in the Citizen of February 10 an article commenting on the fact that General Van Fleet, recently retired as the commander of the army in Korea, says that a big drive now would meet with success. Another general, an acknowledged military expert, Lieutenant General Robert Eichelberger, writing in a magazine, I am not sure whether it is Time or U.S. News and World Report, suggests that the course in Korea cannot be settled by an all-out offensive, but that we have to settle down to a long struggle there and replace in so far as possible some of the United Nations forces with trained and

experienced South Korean troops. He suggests that simply driving to the waist of Korea is not going to be an easy operation, nor will it necessarily end the conflict. Those who have suggested making a drive to the waist of Korea have indicated that that would shorten the line by about half, from 150 odd miles to 70. They think it might be accomplished by suffering a casualty toll of about 50,000 men, but that would be better than to have the thing go on indefinitely, with casualties mounting month by month. But whether anyone is prepared at this stage to advocate such an all-out offensive is something open to question.
Canadian advice and counsel will be needed under these circumstances, and I hope that our people who have the opportunity to make their voices heard will point out some of the difficulties involved in any suggestion of a quick way to end the war in Korea. There is not only the question of the tremendous build-up of material required; there is the question of the training of the troops to take part, and there would be to some extent a frontal attack in addition to any airborne landing or any end runs by naval forces on the flanks; and the rotation system that is being followed by the United States army and by the Canadian brigade rather militates against building up quickly the forces capable of offensive action.
Even if an attempt were made to end the war in Korea, it does not follow that the war in Asia would be completed; for although our forces might be released from Korea, so also would the Chinese armies, unless they were destroyed. They would perhaps then be free to direct greater attention to IndoChina. Perhaps the pinning down of one million Chinese soldiers in Korea has saved southeast Asia from falling into the hands of the communists. If southeast Asia becomes a communist stronghold the whole Far Eastern and south Pacific area will be menaced.
During the past two and a half years the emphasis in our news reports has been on Korea. Malaya has been considered the concern only of the British and Indo-China as a colonial difficulty of the French. Well, consider in that connection the viewpoint of Geoffrey Crowther, editor of the London Economist. I should like to quote from an article that appeared in Look of December 16, 1952, in which he has this to say:
When it comes to comparing relative efforts, Americans tend to overlook what is happening in Malaya, and the French complain even more bitterly that they are given little credit for what they are doing in Indo-China. The British in Malaya and the French in Indo-China, equally with the Americans in Korea, are fighting communists of Chinese nationality, who draw their inspiration and

their weapons from Peking and Moscow. Korea, it is true, is a United Nations war-but only by the accident that the Russians were boycotting the UN when the fighting started and the security council was able to act. To the British and the French, this is a formal distinction but still not a real difference.
The reality is that all three western nations are fighting communism in the Far East, and if the burdens they are shouldering in doing so are pvt alongside their relative resources, the result is nc t as unequal as it can be made to appear by looking at Korea alone. Indeed, there is no doubt that, of the three, the heaviest strain falls on the French, whose contribution in Korea is the smallest.
Let us consider for a moment the effort that has been made in those three areas of conflict and the losses that have been suffered. In Korea it is estimated that United Nations forces number about 500,000, and enemy forces over a million. In Indo-China the French and Viet Namese have 400,000 under arms and their communist opponents about the same. In Malaya, the British and Malayans with 30,000 regular troops and 100,000 auxiliaries are opposed by communist guerrillas numbering about 5,000 and supported by thousands of communist sympathizers.
Casualties in Korea have been heavy; they have also been heavy in these other areas of conflict. United Nations estimates indicate that in Korea casualties on both sides have gone about as high as two million. Our own Canadian brigade in two years of service in Korea had a casualty list on January 31 of this year of 1,335. The cost of the Korean war to the United States is $7 billion a year. A million tons of supplies per month are consumed.
To call this a cold war or a police action is in my opinion to very seriously misuse the English language, and is psychologically unsound. It breeds complacency and indifference, with a resulting slackness in the field of production of military supplies.
Quite a number of examples could be given of apparent slackness in the production of military supplies, and various news reports indicate that munitions of war and military supplies of all kinds have been diverted from Europe to the Far East. That situation is not as good as it might be. The outstanding example, of course, has been the shortage of ammunition in Korea, which has been both acknowledged and denied from various sources.
I give this just as an example of what the attitude toward the Korean war may cause in connection with the vital matter of supplying munitions of war. I noticed that in January of this year Mr. Arthur Blakely, writing in the Winnipeg Tribune, drew attention to
External Affairs
certain developments during the Christmas recess in regard to the matter. I quote his words:
But there's been some interesting developments during the Christmas recess. They've occurred in Korea and in Washington. When President-elect Eisenhower visited Korea, he found-and was disturbed to find-that U.N. troops were handicapped by ... a shortage of ammunition.
He certainly didn't regard the situation which he found as one which could be regarded as perfectly normal under even "static" war conditions.
And then on February 6 the Montreal Star says this:
Canada has been called in to help remedy the shortage of ammunition for United Nations forces in Korea . . .
The shortage of ammunition in Korea, reported and denied repeatedly for months, has been said to have forced rationing among UN troops at the front, particularly in certain types and sizes of shells ...
President Eisenhower confirmed existence of the general shortage when he returned from his trip to Korea before taking office, promising a speedup in deliveries.
And in the Montreal Star of February 9 I find this article from Washington:
The army indicated yesterday it is making progress toward solving ammunition shortages in Korea.
And farther down:
However, army sources said the situation is unchanged from last December 19, when army officers at a Pentagon briefing revealed that President Eisenhower was dissatisfied with the amount of ammunition available in Korea.
The situation in so far as our own Canadian troops are concerned may be quite satisfactory. The over-all picture of munitions supplies in Korea, if these reports are accurate, obviously has not been satisfactory. I suggest that that slackening of effort in the supply of munitions is due to complacency which we should get rid of.
I have quoted from some sources in that connection. I should like now to draw the attention of hon. members to the comments of Mr. Willson Woodside, military critic for Saturday Night. For the last two years he has been drawing our attention to the threat posed by communist efforts in Indo-China. In the issue of February 7 he relates that struggle to the European scene and points out that the difficulties in completing the plans for the army of the European defence community extend from France's troubles in Indo-China.
Just a short quotation from Saturday Night of February 7:
For, although the European army crisis exploded in Paris, it originated in Indo-China. There, following Lenin's famous saying that the road to Paris and London lies through Peking and Calcutta, and the late Andre Zhdanov's exhortation, in founding the cominform in 1947, that the communists must take the capitalist states in the rear

External Affairs
In Southeast Asia, the Soviets have been bleeding French military power to death.
And he suggests that there we may find communist strategy, and the reason for our difficulties in the formation of the desired European defence army.
Another military commentator whose observations merit close attention is Major General Fuller, one of Great Britain's outstanding authorities on warfare. In an interview with U.S. News and World Report reprinted in Reader's Digest for January he says some things I should like to draw to the attention of the house. He was asked a series of questions, to which he gave the answers indicated in the following:
Q. General Fuller, what is your impression of the present European army?
A. As it stands it is pathetically unreal. It's just a paper army. If Russia should move now, there is no obstacle to her overrunning western Europe except the stubborn geography of the Pyrenees mountain range between France and Spain.
Q. Could the allied forces now in Europe fight an effective withdrawal action if Russia did strike?
A. No. It is anybody's estimate how much they could salvage in men and equipment. But our withdrawal would be disastrous psychologically. We must not wrongly assume that the next war will be like the last-a war of retreat, then liberation and finally unconditional surrender.
Q. Does that mean the military outlook in Europe is hopeless?
A. Not at all. The purpose of rearming is to force the enemy to negotiate on terms favourable to yourself.
And then the following:
Q. Do you look for a shooting war in Europe in the foreseeable future?
A. No. It was Lenin's idea "to postpone operations until the moral disintegration of the enemy renders delivery of the mortal blow easy." In his system, psychological took precedence over military. Today Russia's build-up has two purposes: First, to support her psychological war by a terror barrage, a standing threat to all who oppose it; second, to defend herself should her psychological offensive lead to actual war.
General Fuller has had a reputation for thirty years of competent criticism of military effort and is well worth paying attention to. There is another critic to whom almost every military leader during the last thirty years has paid attention, and that is Liddell Hart. In the February issue of the United Nations World he has an article which anyone who is interested in this problem should read with some care. Liddell Hart needs no words of praise from me because he has been praised by so many in the course of his lifetime. Of him Ivan Maisky, the former Soviet ambassador to London, said:
We regard Liddell Hart as the best military brain in England.
In this article Liddell Hart puts himself in the position of Russia's chief of staff and decides what advice he would give to Stalin if

he occupied that position. No man has played a greater part in directing military doctrine than Liddell Hart, and I drew the attention of the house to the credit given him by the German leaders in the last war for the instruction they had gained from his writings on armoured warfare. Putting himself in the position of Russia's chief of staff, he surveys the world scene from the Russian point of view and decides where he would advise Stalin to strike. It is interesting reading indeed, and if world domination is to result he puts the chief emphasis on Great Britain. I should like to quote briefly from what he says:
"In the first place", I would emphasize, "Russia must make sure that she can annihilate Britain quickly-not so much because of Britain's own power but because of her key position, just off the continent of Europe as a base for American counterattack, particularly with atomic bombs. Secondly, we must be able to see a good chance, an effective way, of paralyzing counteraction by the United States for a lengthy period. It will not be enough", I should say, "to overrun Europe and sweep the Americans out of it, unless we can ensure ample time for them to cool down, in a state of impotence, and come to the conclusion that there is more to lose than to gain by a prolonged and destructive effort to recover their hold on Europe."
Of course he elaborates on these two main objectives. It is interesting to note what he would suggest to Stalin with respect to the Far East if he were his chief of staff. He says:
In the Far East, I should use part of our fourth army, which is positioned near the Bering strait, for a raiding stroke against Alaska. That is not a suitable line for a major operation, but even a small stroke there would play on the fears of the Americans and Canadians, and ensure a disproportionate diversion of their forces to guard their own continent.
Finally he concludes with these words:
Nevertheless, I would not care to advise that an attack should be undertaken ... It would therefore be wiser to pursue our "camouflaged warfare" policy and strategy-what our opponents call "the cold war"-which shows many signs of continued and increasing success. As a Soviet soldier, I am profoundly conscious of the fundamental truth of Lenin's maxim, so masterfully applied by Stalin, that "the soundest strategy in war is to postpone operations until the moral disintegration of the enemy renders the mortal blow both possible and easy.
I suggest that Liddell Hart's appraisal of the military scene throughout the world is worth very careful study.
Summing up, what are the courses open to the western democracies? I think we have to pursue our policy of military preparedness. We have to do what we are doing, provide trained men and munitions. In the actual war zone, I think the proper policy is now being employed of training the Korean people themselves and the people in Malaya and Indo-China for service in the field so

they are able to protect their own countries. There is nothing new in that policy because for many years the British and French have trained troops of nations which have been under their control; and if it is pursued the number of United States, British, Canadian and other United Nations forces might reasonably be reduced or might be held in reserve to bolster the homeland forces fighting the enemy. That, plus naval and air support, might be the answer.
In addition, we can supply specialized services from our advanced knowledge of mechanized and scientific warfare. Take the example of South Korea again. It has a population of 20 to 23 million people. They now have 14 divisions trained to operate against the enemy, and could have up to 20. With 20 they might successfully conduct their defensive war against the pressure of the communist forces. In Indo-China similar steps are being taken to train the soldiers of the Viet Nam, and also in Malaya.
In the third place, I think we have to continue our efforts to reach a peaceful settlement. I am not suggesting that such efforts should not be carried on. I have no intention of appearing to be an alarmist. Looking at this problem in an objective manner, I think we are facing the application of force by the communist powers in some parts of the world, and we must attempt to arrive at a peaceful settlement in so far as we can. I hope that a peaceful settlement may be achieved. I hope we will spare no effort to reach a peaceful settlement, but coupled with that I think must go the military preparedness that I have mentioned.
Then, if we follow General Fuller, we must emphasize psychological warfare. General Fuller suggests that that is a part of the communist threat to the world, and he thinks that we have not taken as active a part in that aspect of the conflict as we should. General Fuller was asked this question:
Is there any strictly military answer to communism?
This is his reply:
Certainly not. You must answer an idea with a better idea. In the last two wars, the winners came off almost as badly as the losers. In other words, the power to destroy is rapidly becoming the deterrent to war. Since mankind will continue to argue, the people of the world will more and more be restricted to a psychological battleground in order to avoid extermination.
In all of this what is Canada's part? I suggest that once again in the course of our history we have to become the arsenal of democracy. Our productive capacity and our skill are equal to the task. I think that our armed commitments can be kept on a limited
External Affairs
basis as at present. I agree with the proposal put forward last year by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) that our emphasis should be on air, and that in addition we should supply naval and army forces, but that we should be careful to keep our air fleets in being and not distribute them throughout the world. As far as our army commitments may be concerned, mobile armoured forces should be the answer in this present era, with airborne troops available for quick and useful service in times of emergency. In addition, if we can assist South Korea, IndoChina and Malaya by military teams to train their men, so much the better; and in conjunction with the people of those countries we can put forth a proper and full effort against the menace which appears to be threatening our very existence.
I will conclude, Mr. Speaker, by quoting from President Eisenhower's message to Congress. These are his words:
Our country has come through a painful period of trial and disillusionment since the victory of 1945. We anticipated a world of peace and cooperation. The calculated pressures of aggressive communism have forced us, instead, to live in a world of turmoil.
From this costly experience we have learned one clear lesson. We have learned that the free world cannot indefinitely remain in a posture of paralysed tension, leaving forever to the aggressor the choice of time and place and means to cause greatest hurt to us at least cost to himself.
I would say, Mr. Speaker, that some rethinking of the world situation is required at the present time. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) has pointed out that it is a global problem, and it is on that global scale that we must look at it. I think if we call the war in Asia what it is a war-and consider that our troops in Europe and elsewhere are performing functions that were performed centuries ago by the Roman legions on the borders of that empire; and if we meet the menace of communism which tries to subvert democratic governments, and conduct as far as we are able a modern psychological warfare, then some of our problems in connection with the menace of communist tyranny may be lessened.

Mr. Speaker, I am conscious of the fact that this has turned out to be a long debate, and I can assure you that I will try to shorten my remarks as much as possible or at least to speak as quickly as I can.
It seems evident from what has been said by those who have preceded me in this debate so far that there is very great importance attached by members in this house to the United Nations Organization. Indeed, I believe it is our only hope today for peaceful settlement of the difficulties of the world. I

External Affairs
think there is a primary consideration which must be kept in mind at all times, and it is that the existence of the United Nations is mainly dependent on the support of the people themselves in the other democracies of the world. It is of primary importance that the people themselves should fully understand what the United Nations Organization is and fully appreciate what it can do for them, so they will continue to give it their full support.
As we all know, the United Nations Organization is an association of nations and, as such, is an association of governments. In the case of democracies, governments can only go as far as the people in those countries will allow them to go. It follows that the United Nations can only succeed to the extent that the people in the various countries will allow them to go. So, Mr. Speaker, I think it is of primary importance that we all do our utmost to try to explain and give full appreciation to what this United Nations organization is, to the people in our various constituencies. By the same token I think it is our duty and I think it is my duty tonight and it is the reason that I rise in my place tonight, to answer unfounded criticisms, some of which have appeared in my constituency.
A few weeks ago the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) held a political meeting in my constituency. Naturally I do not know what transpired at the meeting, but when he departed to return to Ottawa he left in his wake an article which was published last week in the local newspaper of one community. It is a very damaging article, in my humble opinion. I think it is one so full of inaccuracies that it cannot go unchallenged, and that the record must be put straight. I refer to an article entitled "An honest appraisal of the United Nations Organization by E. G. Hansell, M.P." The article reads in part as follows:
Truth campaign
Not so long ago President Truman decided on a campaign of truth to expose the evils of communism and went so far as to set up a government agency for this purpose. But truth is not onesided. The searchlight of truth should also be turned upon ourselves, for it is we of the free nations of the UN who are in a pickle at the present time.
I might pause, Mr. Speaker, to wonder for a moment exactly what this means. Since there are only two sides in this issue, the democracies on one side and the communist states on the other, apparently it is we who are in the pickle. I would just refer the hon. member to the excellent speech of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), more particularly at page 1848 of 
Hansard of February 11 where, in talking about the Korean resolution before the United Nations, he summarized as follows:
Their summary rejection, and it was a summary rejection by the communists, of this great opportunity for peace exposes the hollowness and hypocrisy of the communist clamour for a cease-fire without an armistice . . .
Then I go on with the newspaper article:
-truth is still our weapon, but let us have the whole truth.
And here is the first line of his next paragraph:
The fact of the matter is that this United Nations is largely a socialist-communist organization.
Well, Mr. Speaker, one can only go to the history of the organization itself. As we well know the organization arose principally from the Atlantic charter, and I would like to quote a paragraph of that charter which was drawn up in August of 1941 by President Roosevelt and Prime Minister Churchill on a warship on the Atlantic-and there was no socialist-communist there. The paragraph reads:
-a peace which will afford to all nations the means of dwelling in safety within their own boundaries, and which will afford assurance that all the men in all the lands may live out their lives in freedom from fear and want.
Then on January 1, 1942, representatives of 26 nations signed in Washington the declaration by the United Nations expressing support of the principle of the Atlantic charter and pledging their countries to go on fighting alongside each other until victory. So there is nothing socialist or communist in the first history of the organization.
Then we must look at the present membership of the organization. As all hon. members know there are at present 60 nations which are members of the organization. Of those there are 6 nations that can be termed communist and possibly half a dozen that can be termed socialist. So there are now some 48 nations out of 60 which can by no stretch of the imagination be called socialist-communist nations.
It is difficult to understand the ignorance of a member who could make a statement of that nature, that the United Nations Organization is a socialist and communist organization. Even if the implication there was that the U.S.S.R. wanted to tailor the United Nations to their own political pattern, certainly they have not had much success so far. One need but look at the pattern of the voting that has taken place from day to day in the United Nations assembly to see that the pattern is always the same. Take the vote on the Korean issue,

54 nations for and 5 against with one abstention. There was a majority of 49 nations against the 5 nations of the communist-socialist world. I know from personal experience when I was there that that is the pattern all through; inevitably that was the way the vote was recorded. It is, therefore, absolutely unexplainable to me how a member in this house could make a statement of that nature.
Then he goes on in the next sentence:
It is applauded by the internationalists, most of whom are socialists.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not know exactly to whom the hon. member refers as "internationalists". I do know this, that the United Nations Organization-we have had an excellent demonstration in this	house-is
applauded by people of good will throughout the world who are seeking an international basis for justice, harmony and freedom. It is simply ridiculous, for instance, to call the government of Canada socialist, or the government of the United Kingdom. The most important nation in the United Nations and the one that is carrying the biggest load of all is the United States of America, and it is not socialist. It is difficult to understand how anyone could say that the association of these nations is applauded by internationalists. Then the next sentence is as follows:
It was conceived and brought into existence by those who visualized a world government and whose desire, in the process, was to bury national sovereignty-
I must pause on the first part of that sentence, "It was conceived". Possibly the hon. member can do some mind-reading, and is the only one who can tell us the secret aims of the founding fathers. But we do have the nature and purposes of the organization well set out in the charter itself. Anyone, particularly the hon. member who stated that this wias supposed to be an honest appraisal of the United Nations, should have taken the trouble to read the preamble of the charter before judging the organization he was going to appraise. We find the following in a paragraph of the preamble:
-to reaffirm faith in fundamental rights, in the dignity and worth of the human person, in the equal rights of men and women and of nations large and small-
World government, Mr. Speaker; that is exactly what the United Nations is not. It never was intended to be a world government, and that is clearly stated in the charter. All you have to do is turn to article 1, subsection 2, to find t/he following purpose set out:
To develop friendly relations among nations based on respect for the principle of equal rights and self-determination of peoples-
External Affairs
Then, turning to article 2, subsection 1, we find that the organization is based on the principle of the sovereign equality of all its members. In article 2 of the constitution we find set forth the manner in which sovereign rights shall be officially interpreted. We find there that "sovereign equality" was officially defined as meaning that states are juridically equal; that each state enjoys the right inherent in full sovereignty; that the personality of the state is respected as well as its territorial integrity and political independence; that the state should, under international order, comply faithfully with its international duties and obligations.
One turns to section 7 to find the following:
Nothing contained in the present charter shall authorize the United Nations to intervene in matters which are essentially within the domestic jurisdiction of any state or shall require the members to submit such matters to settlement under the present charter-
It is made quite clear in the charter to anyone who cares to read it even in cursory manner that the organization was never intended to be a world government.
Under the heading "Moscow conference" this press report runs something like this:
In 1943 Moscow was the setting for a conference of dignitaries, some of the big men of the earth, none other than the foreign ministers of those nations arrayed against Hitler.
It is not clear if the writer has commendation or condemnation for those who were against Hitler. I continue to quote:
At this conference the setting up of the United Nations Organization was initiated. "The old league of nations had failed. We must have something stronger", seemed to be their theme. It was recognized that in order to have power centralized in a world organization it would be necessary to solidify the already centralized international power of finance, and this would have to be made to synchronize if possible with the proposed United Nations Organization.
It is not quite clear what is meant by the international power of finance. It would seem to indicate that the member sees a dark plot by big bankers to centralize the financial powers of the world. Here again I should like to direct the attention of the house to this organization, the international monetary fund and the bank. The purpose of this organization is just the opposite. It is not a matter of centralizing, because again it is an association of nations and not of individuals. It takes power away from individuals and places it in the hands of nations and governments.
The purposes of the international monetary fund are clearly set forth in the charter of that organization as well. It is to promote international monetary co-operation through a permanent institution which provides machinery for consultation and collaboration

External Affairs
on international monetary problems; to facilitate the expansion and balanced growth of international trade, and to contribute thereby to the promotion and maintenance of high levels of employment and real income and to the development of the productive resources of all members as primary objectives of economic policy; to promote exchange stability; to assist in the establishment of a multilateral system of payments in respect of current transactions between members and in the elimination of foreign exchange restrictions which hamper the growth of world trade; to give confidence to members by making the fund's resources available to them under adequate safeguards, and so on. So, instead of centralizing power, the purpose of this association of nations is to help the less favoured nations.
Then we go on to the next phrase in this report:
The next items on the agenda of the world socio-eommio planners were the Bretton Woods and Dumbarton Oaks conferences which resulted in setting up the international monetary fund and the world bank.
This is a new word which was coined, I presume, for the occasion: "socio-commio" planners. I imagine it means something like socialist communist planners. Here again it is not quite clear who are those planners, but we know that this was planned by the four big nations of the world.
Who were present when these arrangements were made? I am sure we will not find any socialists or communists outside of the one delegation. Representing China was Wellington Koo, who brought China into the league of nations, and Victor Hoo. Representing the United Kingdom was Lord Halifax and Sir Alexander Cadogan. Representing the United States was Edward Stettinius, James Dunn and Joseph Clark Agnew, the latter being a member of the board of review, atomic energy, of the United States. There again there is no indication or at least no substance to the allegation that these were socio-commio planners. It then goes on to say:
These aforementioned agreements were ratified by the parliaments of the signatory nations of the world. But let us pause for a moment and meditate on the startling fact that the executive secretary of the aforementioned conferences and a key figure in shaping this centralized and powerful world financial machinery was none other than Alger Hiss, since convicted by the Supreme Court of the United States as a communist agent. Is it conceivable that such a brain whose first loyalty was to Moscow would advise such machinery as would be contrary to the wishes of the Kremlin?
Reference is made there to a key figure. As all members well know, the bank and the fund were planned at the Bretton Woods

conference. There is no record that Hiss ever attended that conference, either as a member of the United States delegation or on the secretariat. The secretary general of that conference was Mr. Warren Kelchner, chief of the division of international conferences of the state department. There is no evidence whatsoever to indicate that Alger Hiss attended that conference in any capacity whatsoever. He then goes on to say:
Some of Hiss's advisers were men who were already powerful figures in world finance. Among them was Henry Morgenthau, Jr., whose plan to restrict and demoralize the German economy for the benefit of American financiers has back-fired. There was also James P. Warburg who is an ardent advocate of world government. His friend, Eugene Meyer, another powerful banker, became the first head of the International Bank. His successor was John J. McCloy, who sat under the teaching of the marxist Felix Frankfurter of Harvard Law School.
For an hon. member to suggest seriously that Henry Morgenthau, Jr., secretary of the United States treasury and chairman of the United States delegation to Bretton Woods, the elected president of that conference, was an adviser to a middle-ranking civil servant at the conference is beyond all imagination. It is obvious that the writer has indulged in a little indirect anti-semitism. He refers to McCloy, and was attempting to link him up with what he termed was the marxist, Felix Frankfurter. It is quite obvious that this was an unadulterated smear on a very notable person, a justice of the United States supreme court. I cannot say the word I would like to use. Then he goes on:
The same traitor Alger Hiss was also executive secretary of the San Francisco conference and one of the brains behind the charter which moderately advocates a world police force which would whip into line such nations who dared to refuse to toe the line, which line would be determined by the world government boys.
The same traitor, Alger Hiss, is indicated as one of the brains behind the charter. As we all know, the executive secretary of the San Francisco charter was responsible for the administrative arrangements for the conference. There' is no evidence whatsoever to substantiate the statement that he was in any way the brains of the conference. I can imagine that his time must have been pretty well occupied in arranging the administrative details of such a large conference. Delegations from fifty nations attended that conference and drafted the charter.
From Canada there were Mr. Mackenzie King and the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). Then there were Mr. Wellington Koo; Mr. Bidault and Mr. Pleven from France; Mr. Fraser from New Zealand;

Field Marshal Smuts from South Africa; Mr. Eden, Mr. Attlee and Lord Halifax from the United Kingdom, and Mr. Stettinius, Mr. Hull and Senators Connally and Vandenberg from the United States. To suggest that all those men were simply hoodwinked by a member of the secretariat is just fantastic, to say the least. Then he goes on to say:
Oh, yes! And we mustn't forget another choice morsel. Mr. Stettinius was secretary of state of the United States at the time and played a big part in the San Francisco conference. His speeches at this conference were written by one Dalton Trumbo, who has since been exposed as a communist by the congressional committee on unAmerican activities.
The fact that a few United States civil servants in that department have been found unreliable does not justify a statement of that kind as applied to Mr. Stettinius. Frankly this type of slur is most dangerous. Then later on he says:
Why should It be necessary to make surrender of national sovereignty a condition of co-operation?
It is not necessary to surrender national sovereignty to make international co-operation possible. This is not required by the United Nations charter. However, there are instances where freely negotiated and accepted agreements contain terms that limit certain aspects of national sovereignty in the interest of obtaining effective co-operation. Almost any international treaty or agreement involves the voluntary limitation of the exercise of certain rights. The agreement or convention for the suppression of the slave trade or control of the international movement of narcotic drugs required each signatory to agree to a limitation in the exercise of certain rights of sovereignty. There is nobody in this house who would object to such conditions.
I see the clock is moving on, and I do not intend to go any farther with this argument. I think I have quoted enough to show how unreliable and dangerous literature of that nature can be when circulated among the people who go to these meetings, unaware of what is to happen and expecting the truth to be presented to them. I deplore the fact that any hon. member of this house should take advantage of the confidence that was shown in him to spread such propaganda. I repeat that the effectiveness of this vital organization depends in a most essential way on the support which it will receive from the people at large in the democracies.

I did not want to interrupt the hon. member while he was speaking, but perhaps I may ask him a question now. He has been quoting an article which I wrote some time ago, and in asking my question I am not denying that I wrote the article. I 68108-1241
External Affairs
should like to know the name of the newspaper in which it was reprinted, because I did not leave the article there.
The article was published in the local newspaper in the town of Proven-cher where the hon. member for Macleod held a meeting.
What is the name of the paper and of the town?
I will send the hon. member the name.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. J. Browne (Si. John's West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a motion to refer the estimates of the Department of External Affairs to a select committee, and it is the only opportunity hon. members have of speaking on the subject. I therefore wish to take advantage of the occasion to make a few remarks.
A very important event took place last year when the Democratic regime in the United States finished 20 years in office and General Eisenhower, who had been commander in chief of the allied forces in world war II and then had organized the forces in Europe under the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, resigned his position, stood as a candidate and was elected.
It seemed to me that as soon as he announced he was going to run as a candidate, he was going to be elected. There was something about General Eisenhower that impressed the whole world as a man of destiny, a man of the hour. Like Washington, he was first in war, first in peace and first in the hearts of his countrymen.
Although we give credit to General Eisenhower for what he has accomplished up to the present time, I think it would be hard to agree with the leader of the Social Credit group (Mr. Low) in his condemnation of the two previous presidents. On reflection perhaps he will admit that these men made great contributions to the life of the United States and the life of the world, and must not be condemned because they made mistakes. Sometimes they made them because they received bad advice. It seems to me that the people of the United States and the people of the world owed a great deal to President Roosevelt in those early years when he came to the assistance of Great Britain.
Now that a new regime has taken office at Washington it is only to be expected that there will be some change in their policy. They have been criticizing the Democrats for many years for doing the wrong things, and it is therefore only natural that they should try out their own policy. But in regard to foreign affairs President Truman and President Roosevelt before him said

External Affairs
that they were following a bipartisan policy. An example of that was Mr. Dulles negotiating the treaty with Japan, and he is now secretary of state for General Eisenhower.
As a matter of fact there is very little change in the attitude of the present government towards the countries of Europe and the European defence community and that of the administration that preceded General Eisenhower. I hold in my hand several references which prove that there is very little change at all. President Eisenhower himself said that his policy towards our European allies, if it was not to be exactly new, was also going to be more positive. He said that maximum security against communist aggression required closer co-operation among the nations of western Europe, and that this unity could only be created from within. He bluntly warned:
Our allies would get help in the measure that they strive earnestly to do their full share of the common task.
That was General Eisenhower. But here is a statement by Senator Connally, leader of the Democratic party in the United States, which was made in July, 1952. He said, and I am quoting from a summary of the congressional proceedings in the United States for June and July, 1952:
The defence of Germany of course benefits the Germans themselves more directly than any other nation. The U.S.A. was willing to help any free people defend themselves against totalitarian aggression, but it was not willing or able to carry the whole burden of defending those who were not interested in their own self-defence. The Germans had pledged their best efforts; they had undertaken very heavy commitments and they deserved support.
I hold in my hand the Saturday Review of May 31, 1952. In it is a review of a book by Drew Middleton, the correspondent of the New York Times, called the "Defence of Europe". The review by Frank Altschul is headed: "Diplomacy vs. Resources", and he says:
As another example, Mr. Middleton echoes what we hear from many Europeans, that American impatience with the slow progress toward European integration is, to say the least, not well received. When this is expressed in the form of a threat that, unless the process is speeded up, we may discontinue economic and military assistance altogether, positive resentment is aroused.
I quote that, Mr. Speaker, to show that Mr. Dulles is not saying anything new; he is not announcing or pronouncing any new policy. That was said by the Truman government, and there was no great outcry from my friends to the left at that time.
In regard to Formosa, in the same volume of the congressional proceedings there is a

speech by Mr. J. C. Stennis, a Democratic member of the armed services committee, who said:
They should immediately intensify and extend to the division level the training of Chinese nationalist troops on Formosa, and give the highest priority to fully equipping them as early as possible for use on Formosa and in Korea. If communism was to be stopped in Asia, they must develop Asiatic manpower to do the job, and Formosa was the place to begin. First consideration should be given to the eventual use in Korea of the Chinese nationalist troops now on Formosa.
In Time for February 9, however, they say that a great change has taken place in the Formosan policy. The Truman doctrine contained the Chinese nationalists and kept them on Formosa and the United States had sent only a very small amount of equipment there. That is to be changed, and the present administration believe that greater assistance should be given to the armies of Chiang Kai-shek.
Before the hon. members to my left, the members of the C.C.F. party, spoke in this debate I knew what their attitude was going to be. They have frequently laid down the law in this house, especially in regard to China, and particularly in regard to Chiang Kai-shek. They are undoubtedly opposed to Chiang Kai-shek. They lose no opportunity to criticize him. They see no good in the man or in anybody who has been associated with him. But they do not condemn the Chinese communists. To any fair-minded man looking over the record of China for as long as he can look back, say for the past 25 years, it is obvious that during the regime of Chiang Kai-shek China was a very much healthier place for the majority of the people who were living there than it is at the present time.
Take the missionaries who have been persecuted, who have been arrested and imprisoned and punished for no crimes at all, and sometimes have suffered martyrdom. Some of them have been driven out of the country, and they have partially told the story of what went on. Is there anyone who will deny the truth of the statement that instead of bringing freedom, "the communist liberation army brought abject slavery, utter misery and terrifying fear".
I am referring to an article by Father Craig Strang of the St. Francis Xavier mission, Scarboro Bluffs, a Newfoundlander who was a prisoner in communist China for several years, and who has only recently been released and returned to his home. He has written an article entitled "Journey Into Freedom." He is not the only one who has come back from there telling terrible tales

of the cruelty that has taken place since the communist regime assumed power in China.
It was amusing to listen to the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray) today making the statement that the Chinese are great lovers of the land, and how they are going to outlast all the peoples of the earth-that is, they and the French Canadians. Well, I can believe that about the French Canadians, whom I very much admire. I could believe it, too, about the Chinese under a peaceful regime, but not under anything that has taken place since the communists took over. True, the Chinese are lovers of the land. They are peasants, and like peasants everywhere they love the land. But the communists are going to do in China what they did in Russia. They will take the land from the Chinese and divide it into big plots, and in that event the Chinese will just be labourers with no interest in that land. The produce from the land will go principally to the state. So really my hon. friend has not appreciated what has taken place in China.
But to refer back to the article by Father Strang, he tells how the communist army came into Lishui, where he was stationed. They borrowed the furniture and vehicles, although they never returned them. They borrowed the churches for meeting halls, and the priests were never allowed to return to those churches again. The saying of mass was forbidden, and all church services were prohibited. Priests and nuns were kept as prisoners for years, and had to live on very small rations.
I am sorry that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), acting leader of the C.C.F., is not here at the moment to hear what I have to say. Certainly my friends to my left overlook the policy of the communists. It was not the intention of the communists merely to win the war in Korea. That is only a trifling thing, so far as they are concerned, only a means to an end. Out beyond Korea there is a place called Japan, with 80 million people. That is the prize the Russians have in their minds, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) knows it. That is what they are aiming at. And if they once got hold of Japan it is worth all the rest of Asia to them, because of its tremendous industrial potential and the high intelligence and ability of the Japanese.
If they had control of Japan, as the Americans had, we would see a very different story today. The Americans went in there as peace-loving people to help Japan reorganize
External Affairs
on a democratic basis, and to let her be free and independent so that she might take a new place in the democratic world. If Russia had gone in there it would have been for only one purpose, to foster the idea of speedy world domination.
My hon. friends to my left are neglecting that fact. The communists in China are part of that scheme. Father Strang says that while he was waiting for his train in Hangchow there was a peace delegation going to Tibet. They were waving flags and Russian banners, and singing Chinese and Russian communist songs. And at every demonstration where pictures have been taken we see pictures of Stalin side by side with those of Mao Tse-tung. That man was trained in Moscow; Stalin was his best friend. He would not be where he is today but for Stalin. Chiang Kai-shek had driven him out of China, up into Sinkiang, a small corner of .China, where he had only a few thousand troops. The Russians helped him. They armed him with Japanese equipment and ammunition. They built up his people's army into an army of two million men, and helped him and backed him in every way to defeat Chiang Kai-shek.
Yesterday the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) made reference to the assistance the Americans had given to Chiang Kai-shek. That is very questionable. I do not want to debate the subject now, but I have talked about it before. However, it is not true that Chiang Kai-shek had every assistance from the United States government. That government did not know where it was at the time, because it had so many spies in its midst, such men as Alger Hiss, to whom the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) referred. There were men of that kind in the state department, and discord in the United States government in regard to the aid that should be given to Chiang Kai-shek. But if some people in the United States government had had their way the communists would have gone to Formosa, and United States, United Kingdom and commonwealth interests would have been in greater jeopardy than they are today, because Chiang Kai-shek is still on Formosa. After all, his ideas are similar to ours.
No.

Yes. You cannot condemn all the things Chiang Kai-shek has done, because he has done some good things. As I was about to say, he permitted Christian churches to function there; but they cannot function today in China. Perhaps my hon. friend does not

External Affairs
think that is good. He permitted missionaries to go through the country, and I think they did some good.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, to whom I enjoy listening very much, because he is a fine speaker and forthright in his opinions, said today that we should speak plainly. Well, are we the only ones who are going to be allowed to speak plainly? Can Mr. Dulles speak plainly? Can he say what is in his mind? Is he to be extended the same privilege in that respect that is extended to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre? Perhaps the hon. member was referring to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, because he was at great pains to say that the minister was not speaking plainly yesterday, or as plainly as he spoke a week ago when he referred to the deneutralization of Formosa.
Why should not Mr. Dulles speak out plainly? Consider the contribution the United States government has made to world peace and the rehabilitation of Europe. When we hear that Germany's production today is higher than it was in 1939, and when we hear that France's production is higher than it was in 1939, and that Italy is coming along, and that all those other countries are making headway, we must not forget that it was done through funds supplied by the United States. It was for that reason the increase in production was made possible.
It is very fortunate indeed for Europe that there was in the United States a government interested in the rehabilitation of those countries. And what was it done for? The workingman in the United States, the teacher, the professional man-everybody is making a contribution. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) reminds us here frequently that they pay higher income taxes over there because the exemptions are lower than they are in Canada. The people in that country are paying those heavy taxes to save the world.
I know, and I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre must know, the valuable contributions we in Canada are getting from the United States. We can talk so boldly here in the House of Commons, but we would not talk half as boldly if we did not have the United States at our back. They are building big air bases in Newfoundland, at Goose Bay and in Greenland to protect us as well as themselves. We are getting the benefit of that. It is a wonderful thing that we are allies with them.
I should like the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) to say who should decide in a coalition. President Eisenhower is elected and has to make an inaugural speech. What is he going to do? Is he going

to come over here to consult the Secretary of State for External Affairs about what his policy should be? What would the people who returned him to office say if anything of that kind happened?
That is not enough, mark you. Should he go to all the countries of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and ask each one what he should do? Should he go to all the countries of the commonwealth to learn what he should do? No. He has laid down the policy his government is going to follow, and I think it is a good thing that we have a man with such experience in military matters, at the head of affairs in the United States today.
I know my friends on the left do not approve of military men in important positions, and I feel quite sure they do not approve of General Eisenhower. We have to remember that the government of Russia is following ideas for world domination developed by Lenin and Marx. This is a revolution which they want to spread over the whole world. They feel they have a messianic work to do. They want to conquer the whole wide world. Nobody else can live on the earth and have an idea except the Russians. Nobody is allowed to have any other ideas in countries dominated by Russia today. You cannot go and preach social credit in Poland or Czechoslovakia.
Is my hon. friend trying to say that any member of this group agrees with Stalin or his internationalist policy? If so, I think he has not listened to the speeches we have made.
I have not heard you say much against them.
I do not know how anybody could say any more against them than the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Mac-Innis) did.

I do not
agree altogether with what the hon. member is saying now. I know he has said a lot more against Chiang Kai-shek than he has against Mao Tse-tung.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the hon. member would permit a question. When he means the C.C.F. would he mind saying the C.C.F., because the Social Crediters are on his left, too. We certainly do not want to be put in the same category as the C.C.F.

I do not
think anyone would associate the two parties.
Further left.
People reading Hansard do not know whom the hon. member means when he refers to his friends on the left.
I shall remember that in future.
Thank you very much.

We had a
beautiful speech from the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) about his trip. I am delighted to see that so many members on the government side of the house are getting these trips to foreign countries and are improving their knowledge as they are doing. It was a very interesting account. I was not here when he spoke, but I read his speech and it was very interesting. I am glad to know he is so optimistic about conditions in the Middle East, but I wonder what he has to say about the news in the press today that Soviet Russia has broken off diplomatic relations with Israel. What is his opinion on that? I am sorry he cannot give us the answer at this time.
However, I think we can point out that there is a feud between the Arab states and Israel. Which side are we on? Are we with the Arab states or are we with Israel? During the past month or so Soviet Russia has left no doubt where it stands because of its persecution of the Jews, even to the extent of arresting nine Jewish doctors in Russia and accusing them of having poisoned leaders of the Soviet government. Then there is the persecution of Jews in the satellite countries, and now we have the breaking of diplomatic relations. There is a feud between the Arab nations and Israel and Russia hopes to profit thereby and gain the support of the Moslem world.
I do not know where we are going to get support in the Moslem world. From the accounts I get the English do not seem to be popular there. They have to get out, and the Americans do not seem to be popular although they are there with the best of intentions. Spain, which has been despised as a nation, seems to get along very much better with them than anybody else, because a Spanish mission has just completed a tour of the Arab countries and has made agreements with them. I wish we could do the same.
Then there is the story of the persecution in China to which I referred, and of course in the remarks I was making I could not give anything like a lull representation of what has been going on over there. But I am sure we have all read the accounts of the terrible trials of our missionaries, the sisters and the priests who have gone from this country. That has been repeated in those

Mr. Speaker, I was one who had the privilege of attending the United Nations general assembly as a parliamentary observer, and I feel I should say a few words at this time.
It is a common practice at the present time to have parliamentary delegates from all parties attending and observing the proceedings of the United Nations. I believe that is a good and democratic practice. The British North America Act, drawn up as it was during the nineteenth century, did not anticipate such a world organization or parliament and therefore made no provision for Canadian representatives at such a forum.
I am sure that if it had, it would have set out in its terms a provision that our system of responsible government should be maintained and that the delegates represented on the various committees would be members of parliament of the party in power, directly responsible to the existing government.
It was the practice in the first few years of the United Nations to have representatives of the official opposition, I believe, act as representatives with a voice and a vote in the various committees. It is self-evident that this practice is contrary to our system and could lead to some difficulties by having our delegation perhaps committed to a course that would not be in conformity with the policy of the government. The more realistic practice of sending parliamentary observers to take part and assist in forming policy in the Canadian caucus is a correct one, I feel, and it should be continued. While not actually dictating policy, Her Majesty's loyal opposition is thereby given its rightful opportunity to present its views on foreign policy and to report to the House of Commons upon their return.
I am somewhat at a loss to understand why, with my limited capabilities, more particularly in the field of foreign relations, I

was chosen to attend the United Nations. I suspect that it was because the Prime Minister knows of my early associations and public life prior to coming here, when I was associated almost entirely with the cause of labour. The government, I am sure, realizes the important position which organized labour holds today in our democracy and in our foreign relations. As a group they far outnumber any other class. Labour stands to suffer most in the event of a third world war, with all its horrors and the possible destruction of our entire civilization.
I wish to confine my remarks, however, to a few general observations, and in particular perhaps to my impression of the department as gained by my close association with the personnel during my stay in New York. I feel that the personnel serving the department have been excellent. It is my candid opinion that there is no better diplomatic representation anywhere; and when one considers the weight of its influence and reflects that it comes from a nation of less than 15 million people, I feel that is something of which we may be justly proud. When the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) was raised to the high and honourable position of president of the general assembly, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) succeeded him as leader of the Canadian delegation. His voice was heard with respect and admiration in all debates of importance. Indeed the Indian resolution designed to bring about a cease-fire in Korea was patterned on his statement in the general debate in the ad hoc committee on this particular question.
Further proof of the expertness of Canadian diplomacy can be gained, perhaps, by reading a quotation from the London Economist which sets out in clear terms the way I personally feel about our diplomatic staff and its leadership. The article reads:
If it is permissible to generalize about the diplomatic service of any country, it is probably true to say that the representatives of Canada exercise an influence and enjoy a prestige out of all reasonable proportion to the size of their country or the power which it can wield. One reason lies no doubt, in Canada's economic strength and future promise. Another lies in its peculiarly favourable position as a neighbour of the United States, sharing some of the influence yet exempt from all the suspicions which inevitably gather round the leader of a large alliance. But, when all this is said, a more important reason lies in the personal quality of the men themselves.
I have noted with no little satisfaction that recent press statements have suggested that the Canadian Secretary of State for External Affairs may be offered the post of secretary general of the United Nations to replace Trygve Lie, whose resignation is now pending. Should the security council reach such a
External Affairs
decision, the United Nations would be taking a rather giant stride towards bringing about universal co-operation. The loss of such a statesman to the Canadian people would mean a considerable sacrifice, yet it would not be too high a price to pay in furthering the cause of world peace.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I would be inclined to feel that the criticism of the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) last evening was not entirely justified. While we are now enjoying great prestige among world powers, I think it is somewhat unfair to say that if the rank and file of Canadian people feel that they should criticize some of the policies of the United States they are "yapping dogs continuously barking at everything the United States does". It is not quite fair, in my opinion, to go so far in our condemnation of the United States as did the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) in his address on February 12. On page 1881 of Hansard for that date we find the following:
But, Mr. Speaker, when the full history of these times is written, when all the facts have been brought to light, there will be many people who will say that the past two presidents of the United States have been the great betrayers of humanity.
Just read the rest of it.

Yes, I shall read the rest of it:
To be charitable, as I ought to be, I will say that some of those decisions made at Yalta and Potsdam, some of the secret understandings and agreements that were had with Stalin . . .
I should like to remind the house that Right Hon. Winston Churchill was present at Yalta and Potsdam. Are these men, who led us to victory during the last great war, now to be called the betrayers of humanity?
I think, Mr. Speaker, that is going far beyond-
I did not say that.

-what should be expected from a Canadian representative in this House of Commons. I took the trouble of looking up in the dictionary the meaning of "betray" It means to deliver into the hands of the enemy by treachery or fraud; to seduce.
In the past this debate has been conducted on a very high plane, and I had hoped that it would continue on that high plane. I am sure that was the wish of everyone in the house, but when people go about delivering these veiled criticisms of great men, and when we hear them go out in the country and make speeches and write articles such as the one by the member for Macleod read in the house tonight by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jutras), then I am sure we can no longer expect this debate to remain on such a high plane.

Business of the house
I have made considerable preparation for this speech, and there are a number of other things with which I wish to deal, such as the policy Canada should follow today and some of the issues that are before the United Nations. Since it is now ten o'clock, I would move the adjournment of the debate.
On motion of Mr. Byrne the debate was adjourned.
